section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
hook: One app, one billion users. Why can't a single storage system hold all of its data?
title: One app, five data shapes, no single storage system
body:
A global app with 1 billion users stores five kinds of data, and they pull in opposite directions. **Profiles** are small records read constantly. Photos and videos are huge blobs written once and read many times. Messages are small records written nonstop. Logs and events are append-only and enormous. Analytics and ML data is columnar files read in big scans.

A store tuned for one shape fails another. Size matters less than the **access pattern**.
takeaway: Design for the access pattern, not the byte count.
deeper:
**Read-heavy vs write-heavy:** Profiles are read far more than written, so read latency and caching dominate. Messages flip the ratio: writes arrive constantly, so write throughput and per-user ordering matter most.

**Immutable and huge:** Photos and videos are written once and rarely changed, which makes cheap bulk media and erasure coding attractive. They start hot and cool down over time. Logs and events are append-only streams that need append throughput and cheap retention.

**Scans, not lookups:** Analytics and ML data is read by batch jobs and model training in large sequential scans, so aggregate throughput beats per-request latency.

**Where each lands:** Profiles in a replicated database or key-value store with a cache. Photos in an object or blob store. Messages in a log-structured (LSM) database. Logs in a log system such as Kafka that lands in a DFS or object store. Analytics in a data lake. Five shapes, five homes.

quiz.q: A teammate proposes storing chat messages in the same object store as user photos to save on ops. What breaks first?
quiz.a: Messages are small, write-heavy records needing high write throughput and per-user ordering. An object store is built for large write-once blobs replaced whole, so constant tiny writes fit it badly.

mcq.q: Which trait most separates messages from photos in a billion-user app?
options: Messages are write-heavy small records; photos are write-once large blobs
Messages are larger than photos on average
Photos need strong consistency; messages do not
Photos are append-only logs; messages are immutable
mcq.why: Messages are written constantly in small pieces, while photos are written once and read many times. Opposite access patterns need different stores.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
hook: A storage company much smaller than Google loses hard drives every single day. How many?
title: 13 dead drives a day, and that's a small fleet
body:
Backblaze runs about 301,000 data drives. In 2024 its **annualized failure rate** (AFR), the share of drives that die per year, was 1.57%. That is roughly 4,700 dead drives a year, about 13 a day, at a company much smaller than Google or Meta.

No team of humans can chase that. Software must notice each dead disk and rebuild its data on its own.
takeaway: At scale, a dead disk is a Tuesday, not an incident.
deeper:
**Said in 2003:** The Google File System paper put it plainly: "component failures are the norm rather than the exception." That sentence shaped a generation of storage design.

**What automation must do:**
1. Store data redundantly, with replication or erasure coding, so one loss never loses bytes.
2. Notice the failure without a human.
3. Decide when to rebuild. GFS waited 15 minutes, because most node outages are short.
4. Re-create the missing copies elsewhere, placed so one event cannot kill them all.

**The math it feeds:** The same 1.57% AFR drives back-of-envelope durability estimates. With independent failures and fast repair, three replicas look like almost ten nines. Correlated failures make reality worse, which is why placement matters as much as copy count.

quiz.q: Your fleet grows from 30,000 to 300,000 drives at the same 1.57% AFR. What changes about how you run repairs?
quiz.a: Failures go from about 1 a day to about 13 a day. Manual handling stops scaling, so detection and rebuild must be fully automatic.

mcq.q: Backblaze's 1.57% AFR across about 301,000 drives means roughly how many failures per day?
options: About 13
About 1
About 47
About 130
mcq.why: 1.57% of 301,000 is about 4,700 drives a year, which is about 13 a day.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
hook: Each record is a few bytes: a name, a size, a location. Why does keeping them become a system of its own?
title: Ten billion photos, ten billion 'where is it?' records
body:
Before you can read a photo's bytes, something must tell you which machines hold them. That lookup table is **metadata**: data about data, such as names, sizes and locations. On a laptop it is trivial.

Give 1 billion users ten photos each and you have ten billion objects. Just keeping the list of where each one lives becomes a large distributed database. Scaling metadata is the central problem of distributed file systems.
takeaway: Every read begins with a lookup. Scale the lookup or nothing scales.
deeper:
**Hot and critical:** Every operation touches metadata first, so it is hot. Lose it and the bytes may survive but nobody can find them, so it is critical too.

**The one-machine ceiling:** The HDFS NameNode keeps the whole file system namespace in DRAM. Lookups are fast, but the namespace can only grow as big as one machine's memory, a hard limit at billions of objects.

**Why interfaces differ:** File storage lists its scale limit as "metadata server scaling". Hierarchical directories, rename and listing all need a coordinated view of the tree. Object storage uses a flat namespace of buckets and keys, which spreads across many machines more easily, so its scale limit is "very high". The shape of the namespace decides how far the system can grow.

quiz.q: A new service stores 10 billion small files and keeps every path-to-location entry in one server's RAM. What will limit it first?
quiz.a: The metadata server. The namespace can only grow as large as one machine's memory, and every access hits it, so metadata, not disk space, becomes the ceiling.

mcq.q: Why is file storage's scale limit "metadata server scaling" while object storage's is "very high"?
options: A hierarchical tree needs coordinated metadata; flat keys partition easily
Files are stored on slower media than objects
Object storage keeps no metadata at all
File systems cannot span more than one volume
mcq.why: Directories, rename and listing need a consistent view of the tree. A flat key namespace spreads across machines without that coordination.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
hook: Hard disks hold far more than they did twenty years ago. One part hasn't sped up at all. Why does it matter?
title: Disk arms, flash wear and light speed don't negotiate
body:
Three physical limits shape every storage design. A disk arm moves at the same speed it did twenty years ago, yet disks hold far more data, so each terabyte gets less random access. Flash cells survive only a limited number of program/erase cycles. Light takes real time to cross an ocean, so a copy on another continent is never instant.

No software patch removes these. Good designs route around them.
takeaway: Know which law of physics your design is fighting.
deeper:
**The arm:** A 7,200 RPM drive does roughly 80 random IOPS whether it holds 4 TB or 30 TB. So IOPS per TB falls from 20 to about 2.7. Meta's Haystack photo store hit this wall and bought extra drives just for IOPS.

**The cell:** Each flash cell survives a limited number of program/erase (P/E) cycles. Denser QLC (4 bits per cell) is cheaper but wears faster than TLC (3 bits). Garbage collection adds flash writes behind every app write, spending that budget faster.

**The ocean:** Spreading copies across regions protects against natural disasters and regional control-plane bugs. But every synchronous write to a far region pays the travel time of light.

**The catch:** These limits compound. Every bigger disk makes the arm problem worse, which is why hot data keeps moving to flash.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches one 30 TB HDD as a drop-in replacement for three busy 10 TB drives serving random reads. What's wrong with the plan?
quiz.a: Each HDD does roughly 80 random IOPS regardless of size. One drive replacing three cuts available IOPS by about 3×, so the random-read workload stalls even though capacity fits.

mcq.q: Why has HDD random-access performance barely improved in 20 years?
options: Arm and spindle speeds are mechanical and have not gotten faster
The SATA interface caps drives at 600 MB/s
Denser recording makes each read take longer
Drives spend more time on wear leveling
mcq.why: A random read waits for the arm to seek and the platter to rotate. Those mechanical speeds are unchanged while capacity grew.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
hook: Storing each byte 3 times feels safe. At exabyte scale, what does that habit actually cost?
title: 3× vs 1.33×: the decimal that buys exabytes of disk

stat.label: storage cost cut Microsoft said EC could bring

body:
At big-tech scale, cost dominates. Keeping every byte 3 times means buying 3 exabytes of disk for each exabyte of user data. An efficient **erasure code** at 1.33× needs 1.33 exabytes.

The gap buys servers, racks, power and floor space too. Microsoft said erasure coding could cut its storage cost "over 50%" and its datacenter footprint "by 1/2".
takeaway: At exabyte scale, overhead ratios are purchase orders.
deeper:
**Even small steps pay:** Going from RS(6,3) at 1.5× to Azure's LRC at 1.33× saves 0.17×. On one exabyte, that is 170 petabytes of disk you never buy.

**The hidden cost line:** Cost per GB is not the whole bill. For hot data the real limit is often IOPS per dollar. Meta's Haystack bought extra drives just for IOPS, and its effective replication factor rose from an ideal 3.6× to 5.3×. The jump above 3.6× paid for read rate, not durability.

**The right metric:** Measure cost per useful byte per month. It folds redundancy overhead, capacity bought only for IOPS, and media price into one number. Raw price per GB hides two of the three.

**The catch:** Lower overhead is not free. Erasure coding costs repair traffic, extra I/Os for small writes, and slower degraded reads.

quiz.q: Your team cuts overhead from 1.5× to 1.33× on 2 exabytes of user data. How much raw disk do you avoid buying?
quiz.a: 0.17× of 2 exabytes, about 340 petabytes, plus the servers, power and space to run it.

mcq.q: Per exabyte of user data, how much raw disk does 3× replication need compared with a 1.33× erasure code?
options: 3 EB versus 1.33 EB
3 EB versus 1.5 EB
1.33 EB versus 1 EB
4 EB versus 1.33 EB
mcq.why: Overhead multiplies raw capacity: 3× needs 3 EB per EB of data, 1.33× needs 1.33 EB.

section: Why storage infrastructure is hard at big-tech scale
hook: Most storage designs that fail review don't fail on a clever algorithm. What do they fail on?
title: Four questions that sink most bad storage designs
body:
In a storage design review, ask four questions before anything else. What is the data type and **access pattern**? What is the **durability target**? What is the latency target, including the tail, like p99, the latency the slowest 1% of requests exceed? What does it cost per useful byte per month?

Most bad storage designs fail one of these four, not a clever algorithm question.
takeaway: Ask the boring four questions before debating the clever algorithm.
deeper:
**Access pattern picks the shape:** It decides the interface, block, file or object, and the medium. Small, hot, mutable data wants flash with replication. Large, cold, immutable data wants HDD with erasure coding.

**Durability picks placement:** S3's eleven nines do not come from copy count alone. Correlated failures mean copies must be spread across racks, power domains and zones.

**Latency must include the tail:** SSD garbage collection makes p99 and p99.9 far worse than the median. A request that fans out to 100 devices is likely to hit at least one slow one. A design that quotes only the median is hiding something.

**Cost per useful byte:** This one number folds in redundancy overhead (3× replication vs 1.33× erasure coding), capacity bought only for IOPS, and media price. It catches the cheap-looking design that is actually expensive.

quiz.q: A proposal for a hot user-profile store on HDD quotes only median latency and $0.014 per GB. Which of the four questions does it dodge?
quiz.a: Latency including the tail, and cost per useful byte. The median hides p99, and HDDs serve few IOPS per TB, so drives bought just for IOPS raise the real cost.

mcq.q: Why does the review checklist ask for cost per useful byte instead of cost per raw GB?
options: It counts redundancy overhead and capacity bought only for IOPS
Raw GB prices change too often to compare
Useful bytes exclude metadata, which is free
It lets you ignore media price entirely
mcq.why: Raw price hides replication overhead and idle capacity bought for IOPS. What matters is the cost of each byte of real user data.

hook: Every storage medium makes the same trade. Why does no one just use the fastest one for everything?
title: Six media, one trade: each step down is slower and cheaper
body:
No medium is both fast and cheap, so storage is built from a ladder of them. From the top: **DRAM** (nanoseconds, volatile), persistent memory (Intel Optane, discontinued 2022), NVMe SSD (tens of microseconds, GB per second), SATA SSD (same flash, slower interface), HDD (milliseconds, cheapest online media) and tape (seconds to minutes, cheapest per GB, offline).

Real systems use several rungs at once: hot data high, bulk data low.
takeaway: Don't pick the best medium. Pick the right mix.
deeper:
**Ratios, not specs:** DRAM is about 1,000× faster than NVMe for a random read, and NVMe is about 100× faster than HDD. The ladder spans about six orders of magnitude, from about 100 ns for DRAM to about 10 ms for an HDD random read, and seconds or more for tape.

**Online vs offline:** HDD is the cheapest medium that answers a request immediately. Tape needs a robot to load and wind a cartridge, so it fits only data you keep forever and almost never read.

**Volatile vs durable:** DRAM loses everything when power goes, so it serves as cache and hot metadata, never as the only copy. Persistent memory tried to be fast and non-volatile at once, and lost commercially.

**Mixing in practice:** Google's Colossus keeps bulk data on HDD and adds an SSD cache, with machine learning deciding which data is hot enough for flash.

quiz.q: A team wants to put all data, including ten years of backups, on NVMe to keep things simple. What's the argument against?
quiz.a: Cost per GB. NVMe costs several times more than HDD, and backups are rarely read, so HDD or offline tape serves them just as well at a fraction of the price.

mcq.q: Which medium is the cheapest that can still answer a request immediately?
options: HDD
Tape
SATA SSD
NVMe SSD
mcq.why: Tape is cheaper but offline: a robot must load the cartridge first. HDD is the cheapest online medium.

hook: The fastest storage medium you own forgets everything the moment the power blinks. So what is it good for?
title: DRAM: 100 nanoseconds, gone when the power goes
body:
**DRAM** is main memory. A reference takes about 100 nanoseconds, the fastest rung on the storage ladder. Two catches keep it from holding your data alone. It is **volatile**: lose power and the contents are gone. And it is by far the most expensive medium per GB.

So big systems use DRAM for caches and hot metadata, where speed pays, and keep the durable copy somewhere that survives a power cut.
takeaway: Memory is where data goes to be fast, never where it goes to be safe.
deeper:
**Hot metadata:** The HDFS NameNode keeps the entire file system namespace in RAM. Every lookup is fast, but the namespace can only grow as large as one machine's memory.

**Caches:** DRAM's price per GB is the highest of any medium and swings with the memory market. So caches hold only the hottest data, such as profile records, while the durable copy lives on SSD.

**The durability trap:** A value accepted into one server's RAM cache but not yet written to disk is available but not durable. Readers can see it now. A power loss erases it forever. Any system that acknowledges writes from DRAM alone is trading durability for speed.

**The bar to beat:** DRAM caches in front of NVMe flash were "good enough", which helped push Intel's Optane out of the market.

quiz.q: Your write path acknowledges a user's update as soon as it lands in a cache server's memory. The server loses power a second later. What happened to the update?
quiz.a: It is gone. It was available but never durable: readers could see it, but RAM is volatile and no persistent copy existed yet.

mcq.q: Why is DRAM used for caches and hot metadata rather than as the only copy of data?
options: It is volatile and the most expensive medium per GB
It is slower than NVMe for random reads
It wears out after limited write cycles
It can only be addressed in 4 KB blocks
mcq.why: DRAM is fastest but loses data on power loss and costs the most per GB, so durable data lives elsewhere.

hook: Intel built a storage medium faster than flash that kept data through power loss. It still died. Why?

predict.q: Intel's Optane was faster than NAND flash and survived power loss. Why did Intel wind it down in 2022?
options: Lack of demand: DRAM plus NVMe was good enough
Its cells wore out faster than flash
It could not scale past 1 TB per drive

title: Optane: a better medium that still lost
body:
Persistent memory aimed at the gap between DRAM and flash: nearly as fast as memory, but it keeps data after power loss. Intel sold **Optane**, based on 3D XPoint, from 2017. Optane SSDs had about 9 microsecond latency, and Optane DIMMs were about one order of magnitude slower than DRAM.

Micron stopped 3D XPoint work in March 2021. In July 2022 Intel announced the wind-down, citing lack of demand. DRAM caches plus NVMe flash were "good enough" and cheaper.
takeaway: Better loses to good enough when good enough is cheaper.
deeper:
**The numbers:** Optane as an SSD read in about 9 µs, with GB/s of throughput and a price between DRAM and NAND. NVMe flash reads in roughly 50 to 150 µs. A real improvement, but not enough to justify a new tier for most buyers.

**Why good enough won:** The workloads persistent memory targeted could already be served by DRAM caches in front of NVMe flash. That pairing was cheaper, and buyers did not pay for the gap.

**The senior lesson:** When you evaluate a new medium, the question is not "is it faster?" It is "is the gap over cheap mainstream parts big enough to sustain a market?"

**The catch for designers:** A system built around one vendor's medium carries risk if that medium is discontinued. Optane went from launch in 2017 to wind-down in 2022.

quiz.q: A startup pitches a new memory that is 3× faster than NVMe flash but costs more per GB. Given Optane's history, what's your first question?
quiz.a: Is the gap big enough to beat DRAM caches plus NVMe, which are already good enough and cheaper? Optane was faster too and still died for lack of demand.

mcq.q: What reason did Intel give for winding down Optane in July 2022?
options: Lack of demand
Excessive wear under write-heavy load
A patent dispute with Micron
A security flaw in Optane DIMMs
mcq.why: Intel cited lack of demand. DRAM caches plus NVMe flash were good enough and cheaper for most workloads.

hook: An SSD reads a random page about 100× faster than a hard disk. What does it give up for that speed?
title: SSDs: no moving parts, microsecond reads, a wear budget
body:
A hard disk must swing an arm and wait for a platter to spin before it reads anything. A **solid-state drive** (SSD) stores data in NAND flash chips with no moving parts, so random reads take about 50 to 200 microseconds, NVMe at the lower end.

The price is paid twice. Flash costs more per GB than disk. And its cells **wear out** with writes, so every write spends part of a finite budget.
takeaway: Flash sells speed by the gigabyte and charges again in wear.
deeper:
**The price gap:** Late-2025 consumer NVMe drives of 4 to 8 TB cost roughly $0.05 to $0.10 per GB. Backblaze measured HDDs at $0.014 per GB in November 2022. The years and sources differ, so treat the ratio as rough, but it is why bulk data still lives on HDD.

**The wear budget:** Each cell survives a limited number of program/erase cycles. The drive's own garbage collection adds writes you never asked for, which spends that budget faster.

**Hidden machinery:** Flash cannot overwrite a page in place. Firmware called the flash translation layer remaps every write so the SSD still looks like a normal disk. That machinery explains both SSD wear and occasional latency spikes.

**Where it wins:** SSDs deliver far more IOPS per TB than HDDs, so the industry puts hot, randomly accessed data on flash.

quiz.q: You're choosing media for 5 PB of old, rarely viewed photos and 20 TB of hot user profiles. Which goes on flash, and why?
quiz.a: The profiles. They are small, hot and randomly accessed, where flash's microsecond reads and high IOPS per TB pay off. Rarely viewed photos care about cost per GB, where HDD wins.

mcq.q: What lets an SSD serve random reads so much faster than an HDD?
options: No seek or rotational wait, because nothing moves
A faster SATA interface than HDDs use
Larger pages that hold more data per read
A DRAM cache that holds the whole drive
mcq.why: An HDD pays for arm movement and platter rotation on every random read. Flash has no moving parts, so reads take tens of microseconds.

hook: Two SSDs use the same kind of flash chips. A many-core server can drive one far harder. Why?
title: Same flash, 1 queue vs 65,535: NVMe vs SATA
body:
NVMe and SATA SSDs use the same NAND flash. The difference is mostly the interface. SATA's controller interface, **AHCI**, was designed for hard disks and supports one queue of 32 commands. **NVMe** runs over PCIe and supports up to 65,535 queues of 65,536 commands each.

With one queue, every CPU core lines up at the same door. With thousands, many cores drive the SSD in parallel. New datacenter flash is almost always NVMe.
takeaway: An interface built for one spinning arm starves chips that work in parallel.
deeper:
**Why AHCI looked fine:** A spinning disk serves one mechanical operation at a time, so a single 32-command queue was enough. Flash has many chips that can work at once. A deep, multi-queue interface lets the drive use that parallelism, and each core can have its own queue instead of contending for one.

**Bandwidth ceilings:** SATA 3 tops out near 600 MB/s. A PCIe 4.0 x4 link has a ceiling near 8 GB/s, and PCIe 5.0 x4 near 16 GB/s. A single SATA link can bottleneck flash that could deliver far more.

**Same cells, same price:** SATA SSDs have similar flash latency plus interface overhead, and cost about the same per GB as NVMe. You pay the same and get less.

**In industry:** Meta's 2024 GenAI clusters use high-capacity E1.S NVMe SSDs in their storage servers.

quiz.q: A 64-core database server is I/O-bound on a SATA SSD, yet the flash itself is far from busy. What's the likely bottleneck, and the fix?
quiz.a: The AHCI interface: one queue of 32 commands shared by all cores, over a ~600 MB/s link. NVMe gives many deep queues and a far higher PCIe ceiling.

mcq.q: How many command queues does NVMe support, compared with SATA's AHCI?
options: Up to 65,535 queues vs 1 queue
Up to 32 queues vs 1 queue
Up to 65,536 queues vs 32 queues
Up to 256 queues vs 8 queues
mcq.why: AHCI has one queue of 32 commands. NVMe supports up to 65,535 queues of 65,536 commands each, so cores submit in parallel.

hook: A hard disk takes about 100,000× longer than RAM to fetch a random byte. Where does all that time go?
title: A random HDD read costs ~10 ms: seek plus spin
body:
A **hard disk drive** stores data on spinning magnetic platters. To read, an arm moves the head to the right track, the **seek**, then waits for the right sector to rotate underneath. At 7,200 RPM that wait averages 4.17 ms. Add a seek of several milliseconds and a random read costs roughly 10 ms.

Sequential reads pay that toll once, then stream.
takeaway: A disk streams fast and searches slowly. Shape your I/O to match.
deeper:
**Where 4.17 ms comes from:** At 7,200 revolutions per minute, one turn takes about 8.3 ms. On average the target sector is half a turn away. The seek varies with distance; about 8 ms is a typical average.

**Streaming is different:** Once the head is on track, data flows off the platter continuously. Enterprise drives in the 2020s sustain over 500 MB/s with dual-actuator models, and hundreds of MB/s is typical.

**Designs that follow:** Big HDD-based systems favor large sequential I/O. Dropbox's Magic Pocket writes 1 GB extents, and Azure seals roughly 1 GB extents before erasure coding them.

**The catch:** HDDs are the cheapest online medium, about $0.014 per GB in Backblaze's November 2022 figure. But the mechanics have barely changed while capacity grows, so each terabyte gets fewer random operations every year.

quiz.q: A job reads 1 GB from an HDD as one sequential stream, then again as 250,000 random 4 KB reads. Why is the second run dramatically slower?
quiz.a: Each random read pays a seek plus rotational wait, about 10 ms, so 250,000 reads take about 40 minutes. The sequential read pays that once, then streams at hundreds of MB/s.

mcq.q: At 7,200 RPM, why is average rotational latency 4.17 ms?
options: A turn takes about 8.3 ms and the sector is half a turn away
The average seek takes 4.17 ms
The head reads one full track every 4.17 ms
SATA adds 4.17 ms of interface overhead
mcq.why: 60 s / 7,200 is about 8.3 ms per rotation. On average you wait half of that for the sector.

hook: Overlap a disk's tracks and it holds about 25% more. What rule does that force on every write?
title: SMR: 25% more disk, if you write it like a log
body:
**SMR** (shingled magnetic recording) overlaps tracks like roof shingles. Seagate's first SMR drives in 2013 gave about 25% more capacity. The cost: you cannot rewrite one track without damaging the next, just as you can't replace a middle shingle without disturbing its neighbour.

So the disk is split into **zones** that must be written sequentially, like an append-only log. Host-managed SMR makes the software above the drive respect those zones.
takeaway: A quirky medium is cheap if your software writes the way it wants.
deeper:
**In industry:** Dropbox built its Magic Pocket storage to write 1 GB extents aligned to 256 MB SMR zones. It expected close to 40% of its data to be on SMR by the end of 2019, with more than 20% overall savings versus the previous design.

**Who it suits:** SMR turns a random-write device into something close to an append-only log. That is fine for systems that write large immutable chunks, and painful for workloads that update small pieces in place.

**The same pattern on flash:** Flash cannot overwrite in place either. Log-structured, append-oriented designs fit both SMR zones and flash erase blocks.

**The catch:** With host-managed SMR, the storage software must track zones and write pointers itself. The drive no longer hides the complexity, so you take it on in exchange for the capacity.

quiz.q: You're considering host-managed SMR drives for a database that updates small rows in place all day. What's the problem?
quiz.a: SMR zones must be written sequentially, because rewriting one track damages the next. Small in-place updates break that rule, so the workload fights the drive instead of fitting it.

mcq.q: Why must host-managed SMR zones be written sequentially?
options: Tracks overlap, so rewriting one damages the next
The write laser must cool between writes
Each zone can only be erased as one flash block
Zones share a read head that cannot seek
mcq.why: Shingled tracks overlap like roof shingles. Writing a track disturbs its neighbour, so zones are written in order, like a log.

hook: Hard drives just crossed 30 TB. Why does that make them worse at one of their main jobs?

predict.q: A 30 TB HAMR drive vs a 4 TB drive: how do their random reads per second compare?
options: About the same
About 7× more on the 30 TB drive
About 2× more on the 30 TB drive

title: HAMR: a laser shrinks the bits, 30 TB per drive
body:
Disks grow by packing smaller bits, and tiny bits are hard to write stably. **HAMR** (heat-assisted magnetic recording) uses a tiny laser to heat a spot on the platter while writing, so smaller bits can be written stably. Seagate launched its Mozaic 3+ HAMR platform with 28 TB and 30 TB drives in January 2024.

The arm and spindle stay as slow as ever. Only capacity grows.
takeaway: Bigger drives make cold bytes cheaper and hot bytes harder.
deeper:
**The capacity curve:** Backblaze's fleet added 24 TB drives in December 2024, and HAMR pushes to 30 TB. Backblaze measured HDD cost falling from $0.114 per GB in 2009 to $0.014 per GB in November 2022, roughly an eightfold drop.

**The IOPS squeeze:** A 30 TB HAMR drive still does roughly 80 random IOPS, the same as a 4 TB drive, because its arm and spindle are no faster. IOPS per TB falls from 20 at 4 TB to 6.7 at 12 TB, 3.3 at 24 TB and 2.7 at 30 TB.

**What follows:** Cold, sequentially read data gets cheaper to store. Hot, randomly read data gets harder to serve from disk. That tension is why hot data moves to flash and big HDDs hold warm and cold data read with large sequential I/O.

quiz.q: Your team moves a busy photo index from 12 TB drives to 30 TB HAMR drives, using 60% fewer drives. What happens to random-read capacity?
quiz.a: It drops by about 60%. Each drive still does roughly 80 IOPS, so fewer drives means fewer IOPS, even though total capacity is the same.

mcq.q: How does HAMR let a hard drive hold more data?
options: A laser heats a spot so smaller bits can be written stably
Tracks overlap like shingles to fit more per platter
Two actuators read different platters at once
Platters spin faster to pack bits tighter
mcq.why: HAMR heats a tiny spot during writing, making smaller bits stable. Overlapping tracks is SMR, a different trick.

hook: The cheapest place to keep 40 TB uses zero power and can take minutes to return one byte. Who wants that?
title: Tape: 40 TB a cartridge, zero shelf power, slow to wake
body:
Some data must be kept for years and will almost never be read. **Tape** (LTO) serves it. LTO-10 cartridges hold 30 TB or 40 TB native and transfer at 400 MB/s. Tape is very cheap per GB and uses no power sitting on a shelf.

The catch is the first byte. A robot must load the cartridge and wind the tape, so **first-byte latency** is seconds to minutes. It fits "keep forever, read almost never" data.
takeaway: Tape trades time-to-first-byte for the lowest cost per byte kept.
deeper:
**Offline means offline:** Tape is the bottom rung: lowest cost per GB, and offline. A mechanical process must happen before any byte comes back, which rules it out for anything user-facing.

**Latency vs throughput:** First-byte latency is terrible, but once streaming, 400 MB/s is on par with a fast hard disk. Tape rewards large sequential restores and punishes small random reads.

**Where it lands:** Backups and compliance archives are rarely read, must be kept for years, and need the lowest cost and immutability. They go to an archive object tier or tape, with media being an HDD cold tier or tape.

**The power bill:** A cartridge on a shelf draws no power. Hardware is chosen on power per TB as well as cost and IOPS per TB, a point in tape's favour for archives.

quiz.q: Legal needs seven years of audit logs kept and expects to read them maybe once. Engineering wants them on HDD for instant access. Where should they go?
quiz.a: Tape or an archive tier. The logs are almost never read, so seconds-to-minutes first-byte latency costs little, while tape's low cost per GB and zero shelf power save money every year.

mcq.q: Why is tape unsuitable for serving user photos?
options: First-byte latency is seconds to minutes
Its throughput is below 10 MB/s
Cartridges hold less than 1 TB
It needs constant power to keep data
mcq.why: A robot must load and wind the cartridge before the first byte returns. That is fine for archives, not for interactive reads.

hook: You can forget most storage specs. Which two numbers should you never forget?

predict.q: For a random read, roughly how much faster is DRAM than an NVMe SSD?
options: About 1,000×
About 10×

title: DRAM is ~1,000× NVMe; NVMe is ~100× HDD
body:
Storage specs change every product cycle. The gaps between tiers barely move, so memorize those. A DRAM reference takes about 100 ns. Optane read in about 9 µs. An NVMe SSD reads in about 50 to 150 µs. A 7,200 RPM HDD takes about 10 ms. Tape takes seconds to minutes.

Treat these as orders of magnitude: DRAM is about 1,000× faster than NVMe for a random read, and NVMe is about 100× faster than HDD.
takeaway: Prices drift. Orders of magnitude don't. Reason with the ratios.
deeper:
**The throughput column:** DRAM delivers many GB/s. NVMe's interface ceiling is about 8 to 16 GB/s over PCIe 4.0/5.0 x4. SATA SSDs cap near 600 MB/s with one queue of 32 commands. HDDs do hundreds of MB/s, over 500 MB/s for some enterprise drives. LTO-10 tape does 400 MB/s native.

**The cost column:** DRAM is the highest per GB and swings with the memory market. Consumer NVMe ran about $0.05 to $0.10 per GB in late 2025. HDD was $0.014 per GB in Backblaze's November 2022 figure. Tape is the lowest. The sources and years differ, so read price ratios as rough.

**Using the ratios:** If a design needs thousands of random reads per second per TB, the ratios tell you at once that HDD will not do it. No spreadsheet needed.

quiz.q: A cache miss sends a request from DRAM all the way to an HDD. Using the ratios, roughly how many times slower is the miss than the hit?
quiz.a: About 100,000×. DRAM is about 1,000× faster than NVMe, and NVMe about 100× faster than HDD: roughly 100 ns versus 10 ms.

mcq.q: Why are ratios between tiers more useful than exact latency figures?
options: Exact figures shift with generations; the gaps between tiers stay stable
Vendors publish only ratios, not figures
Ratios include the cost of the interface
Exact figures are always within 10% anyway
mcq.why: Specific numbers change with hardware generations and markets. The order-of-magnitude gaps between tiers stay stable enough to reason with.

hook: The hard drive won the price-per-GB comparison. Six months later it's the expensive option. What went wrong?

predict.q: An HDD costs far less per GB than an SSD. For a hot, random-read workload, which usually costs less per useful byte?
options: Often the SSD
Always the HDD
They always come out the same

title: A cheap HDD that can't serve your reads isn't cheap
body:
The common mistake is comparing SSD and HDD only on cost per GB. For hot data, the real limit is often **IOPS per dollar**: how many I/O operations per second each dollar buys. An HDD does roughly 80 random IOPS no matter how big it is.

If your workload needs more reads than the disks can serve, you buy extra disks just for IOPS and leave their capacity empty. The per-GB bargain evaporates.
takeaway: Price the resource you run out of first.
deeper:
**In industry:** Meta's old hot-photo store, Haystack, became IOPS-bound. IOPS per drive stayed flat while drive capacity grew, so Meta bought extra drives just for IOPS. Its effective replication factor rose from an ideal 3.6× to 5.3×. The jump above 3.6× paid for read rate, not durability.

**Pick the metric per workload:** For cold, sequentially read data such as backups, old photos and analytics scans, cost per GB dominates and HDD wins. For hot, randomly accessed data such as profiles, messages and fresh uploads, cost per IOPS dominates and flash often wins despite a higher sticker price.

**The fixes industry uses:** Keep hot data on flash. Keep big HDDs for warm and cold data with large sequential I/O. Mix IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks, as Meta's Tectonic does, so neither resource sits idle.

quiz.q: A workload needs 8,000 random reads per second over 20 TB. Someone proposes one 24 TB HDD. How many HDDs does the read rate actually demand?
quiz.a: About 100. Each HDD serves roughly 80 random IOPS, so 8,000 IOPS needs about 100 drives, leaving most of their capacity empty. Flash is likely cheaper here.

mcq.q: For hot, randomly read data, which metric usually decides between SSD and HDD?
options: IOPS per dollar
GB per dollar
Sequential MB/s per dollar
Watts per GB
mcq.why: Hot data is limited by random reads. HDDs deliver few IOPS each, so buying enough of them wastes capacity and money.

hook: An SSD can write a single 4 KB page but cannot overwrite it. What does it do when you change one byte?
title: Flash writes pages but erases only whole blocks
body:
NAND flash reads and writes in **pages** of about 2 to 16 KB, grouped into **blocks** of about 128 to 256 pages. A page cannot be overwritten. It must be erased first, and erase works only on a whole block.

So changing one page in place would wipe up to 255 neighbours. The SSD never does that. An "update" writes the new data to a fresh page and marks the old page stale.
takeaway: Flash never edits. It rewrites elsewhere and cleans up later.
deeper:
**An analogy that maps:** Think of a whiteboard you can write on one small square at a time, but can only wipe a whole panel at once. Squares are pages; the panel is a block. To change one square, you write the new version in a clean square and cross out the old one.

**Three consequences:**
1. Something must track where each logical piece of data lives now: the flash translation layer.
2. Stale pages pile up, so the drive must copy valid pages out of a block and erase it: garbage collection.
3. Those copies are writes the host never requested: write amplification, which wears cells and competes with your I/O.

**Why logs fit flash:** Append-oriented, log-structured designs naturally write new data sequentially instead of updating in place, which is exactly what flash wants.

quiz.q: An app rewrites the same 4 KB record 1,000 times on an SSD. Before any cleanup runs, how many physical pages have held a version of it?
quiz.a: About 1,000. Each update goes to a fresh page and the previous one is marked stale. Only the newest is valid; the rest wait for garbage collection.

mcq.q: Why can't an SSD update a flash page in place?
options: Pages must be erased first, and erase works only on whole blocks
The FTL locks pages after their first write
Pages become read-only once the drive is 80% full
Each page can be written only once in its lifetime
mcq.why: Erasing one page would mean erasing its whole block of 128-256 pages, destroying valid data. So updates go to fresh pages.

hook: Flash can't overwrite anything, yet your OS rewrites the same disk address all day without noticing. How?
title: The FTL: firmware that fakes a rewritable disk
body:
The OS thinks it rewrites address 7 in place. Flash forbids that. The **flash translation layer** (FTL), firmware inside the SSD, bridges the gap. It maps logical block addresses, what the OS sees, to physical pages, where data really sits.

On every overwrite the FTL writes to a fresh page and updates the map. That is why an SSD looks like an ordinary disk from outside.
takeaway: Every clean abstraction hides a busy machine. Benchmark the machine.
deeper:
**More than a map:** The FTL is the SSD's own little storage system. Besides address mapping it runs garbage collection, reclaiming blocks full of stale pages, and wear leveling, spreading program/erase cycles evenly so no block dies early.

**The price of hiding:** The host cannot see when the drive is busy with internal work. A read that lands on a chip in the middle of an erase simply waits. From outside it looks like a random latency spike, which is why SSD tail latency can be far worse than the median.

**It depends on state:** FTL behavior changes with how full the drive is, how much over-provisioned spare it has, and the write pattern. Small random overwrites on a nearly full drive make it copy the most. So benchmark drives that are 80% full and written to steady state. Fresh drives haven't made the FTL work yet.

quiz.q: Two identical SSDs run the same read test. One is new; the other is 80% full after months of random writes. Why might the old one show worse p99?
quiz.a: Its FTL must garbage collect constantly, copying valid pages and erasing blocks. Reads that land on a chip busy erasing wait. The new drive has free blocks and barely collects.

mcq.q: What does the flash translation layer map?
options: Logical block addresses to physical flash pages
Files to directories in the file system
Physical pages to DRAM cache lines
Erase blocks to host-managed SMR zones
mcq.why: The OS addresses logical blocks. The FTL maps each to the physical page holding the data and remaps it on every overwrite.

hook: Your SSD writes data you never sent it. Where do those extra writes come from, and who pays?
title: Garbage collection: the SSD writes you never asked for
body:
Updates leave stale pages behind, so blocks slowly fill with a mix of valid and dead data. To free space, **garbage collection** (GC) copies the still-valid pages elsewhere, then erases the whole block.

Those copies are writes the host never asked for. A mostly stale block is cheap to reclaim. A mostly valid one means copying nearly all of it to free a few pages.
takeaway: The cheapest block to clean is the one that's already mostly garbage.
deeper:
**What makes GC expensive:** A nearly full drive has few free blocks, so GC must pick victims that still hold many valid pages. Small random overwrites scatter stale pages across many blocks instead of freeing whole blocks at once. Large sequential writes tend to invalidate whole blocks together, leaving little to copy.

**Bill one, wear:** Every copied page is an extra flash write. That multiplies total writes, measured as the write amplification factor, and spends the cells' limited program/erase cycles faster.

**Bill two, latency:** GC reads, writes and erases on the same flash chips your application uses. A read that lands on a chip busy erasing must wait, and that wait shows up in p99.

**One cause, two symptoms:** Shorter drive life and tail latency spikes come from the same mechanism. Fix the write pattern and you help both.

quiz.q: A logging service writes large sequential files; a metadata service does small random overwrites on a nearly full drive. Which SSD does more garbage collection per byte written?
quiz.a: The metadata service's. Its scattered updates leave many blocks partly valid, so GC copies lots of live pages to free each block. Sequential writes invalidate whole blocks together.

mcq.q: Why does garbage collection cause SSD latency spikes?
options: It uses the same flash chips as foreground I/O
It pauses the host CPU during erases
It flushes the OS page cache
It sends data over the SATA link twice
mcq.why: GC copies and erases on the chips your reads need. A read that lands on a busy chip waits much longer.

hook: Your app wrote 1 GB to an SSD. The flash chips inside wrote more. How much more, and why?

predict.q: Your app writes 1 GB of small random overwrites to a nearly full SSD. How much can the flash itself end up writing?
options: Several GB, such as 3 GB
Exactly 1 GB
Less than 1 GB, thanks to compression

title: Your app wrote 1 GB. Your SSD wrote 3.
body:
Flash can't overwrite a page, and erase works only on whole blocks. So garbage collection copies still-valid pages out of a block before erasing it. Those copies are writes nobody requested.

The ratio has a name: **write amplification factor** (WAF), bytes written to flash divided by bytes written by the host. A WAF of 3 means every 1 GB your app writes becomes 3 GB inside the drive. Small random overwrites on a nearly full drive give the worst WAF.
takeaway: The write you send is not the write the flash pays for.
deeper:
**The levers:** Large sequential writes tend to invalidate whole blocks together and keep WAF near its minimum. Over-provisioning, spare flash hidden from the host, lowers WAF because GC can pick blocks with fewer valid pages to copy.

**Bill one, lifetime:** Endurance really comes down to flash program/erase (P/E) cycles. Drives are rated in TBW (terabytes written) or DWPD (drive writes per day). At WAF 3, your app's writes wear the flash 3× faster than their size suggests, so you hit the TBW rating early.

**Bill two, latency:** GC runs on the same flash chips as your reads. Most reads take about 100 µs, but one that lands on a chip busy erasing waits much longer. The median looks great; the p99 does not.

**The catch:** One number, two bills. A high WAF usually means both a shorter drive life and a worse tail.

quiz.q: Two apps write the same volume to identical SSDs. One does large sequential writes; the other, small random overwrites on a nearly full drive. Which drive wears out first and has worse p99?
quiz.a: The random-overwrite drive. Its blocks stay partly valid, so GC copies more (higher WAF), spending P/E cycles faster and competing with reads on the same chips.

mcq.q: An SSD's WAF is 3. What does that mean?
options: Each 1 GB the host writes causes 3 GB of flash writes
The drive's TBW rating is divided by 3 for reads
Each page is written to 3 separate blocks for safety
One-third of flash capacity is hidden as spare
mcq.why: WAF is flash bytes written divided by host bytes written. The extra 2 GB are garbage-collection copies.

hook: Storing one more bit in each flash cell makes the SSD cheaper. What do you pay for that extra bit?
title: 4 bits vs 3: QLC is cheaper, TLC lasts longer
body:
Each flash cell survives only a limited number of **program/erase (P/E) cycles** before it wears out. Packing more bits into a cell lowers the price per GB but wears faster: QLC (4 bits per cell) has lower endurance than TLC (3 bits).

The firmware fights uneven wear with **wear leveling**, spreading P/E cycles evenly so no block dies early. Drives advertise endurance as TBW (terabytes written) or DWPD (drive writes per day).
takeaway: Cheap flash is fine for data that's read, not rewritten.
deeper:
**Ratings vs reality:** The real limit is P/E cycles on the flash, not the bytes your app sends, and write amplification sits between the two. If an app writes 1 TB a day at WAF 3, the flash absorbs about 3 TB. It wears three times faster than the app's own write volume suggests, so the drive hits its TBW rating early.

**Choosing a cell type:** QLC's extra bit per cell lowers price per GB, which suits read-mostly or cold data on flash. TLC's higher endurance suits write-heavy workloads, such as messages written constantly.

**Why leveling matters:** Workloads are uneven. Without wear leveling, a few hot logical addresses would hammer the same physical blocks until they failed while most of the drive stayed fresh. The FTL remaps writes across all blocks so the whole drive ages together.

quiz.q: A message store writes 2 TB a day to SSDs at a WAF of 3. QLC or TLC, and why?
quiz.a: TLC. The flash absorbs about 6 TB of writes a day, and TLC survives more P/E cycles. QLC's lower endurance would wear out far sooner under that load.

mcq.q: Why does QLC flash wear out faster than TLC?
options: Storing 4 bits per cell instead of 3 lowers endurance
QLC firmware has no wear leveling
QLC pages are erased one at a time, not in blocks
QLC drives have no over-provisioned spare
mcq.why: More bits per cell is cheaper but tolerates fewer program/erase cycles, so QLC has lower endurance than TLC.

hook: An SSD benchmark shows a great median read time. Your users still see slow requests. Where's the gap?
title: Why SSD p99 looks bad while the median looks great
body:
Most SSD reads take about 100 µs. But garbage collection competes with your I/O for the same flash chips, and a read that lands on a chip busy erasing a block waits much longer. The median looks great. The **p99** or p99.9, the slowest 1% or 0.1% of requests, looks bad.

Those slow outliers are **tail latency**, a direct side effect of the drive's hidden cleanup work.
takeaway: Users don't feel your median. They feel your slowest dependency.
deeper:
**Fan-out makes it worse:** One user request may read from 100 devices in parallel and must wait for the slowest. Even if each device is slow only rarely, at least one of the 100 being slow becomes likely. The request's latency tracks the devices' tail, not their median.

**Two ways to fight it:**
1. Hedged reads: send a backup request if the first is slow, and take whichever returns first.
2. Reconstruction: with erasure coding, rebuild the needed data from other fragments instead of waiting on the slow one.

**In industry:** Azure does the second. If a fragment read looks slow, it starts a reconstruction in parallel and returns whichever finishes first.

**State matters:** A nearly full drive under mixed reads and writes does more GC than a fresh one, so tests on new, empty drives understate the tail.

quiz.q: Each storage device is slow on 1 read in 100. A page load reads from 100 devices in parallel. Roughly how often is the page load slow?
quiz.a: Most of the time, about 63%. The chance all 100 are fast is 0.99^100, about 37%. The request follows the tail, not the median.

mcq.q: How does Azure cut tail latency when a fragment read looks slow?
options: It reconstructs the data from other fragments in parallel
It retries the same fragment until it responds
It moves the fragment into DRAM
It pauses garbage collection on that drive
mcq.why: Azure starts a reconstruction from other erasure-coded fragments in parallel and returns whichever finishes first.

hook: A vendor's SSD benchmark looks flawless. Which conditions would make it tell the truth?
title: Ask for p99.9 on a full, steady-state drive
body:
Design for the tail, not the median. When someone shows you an SSD benchmark, ask for **p99.9** latency, the time only 0.1% of requests exceed, under mixed read/write load, on a drive that is 80% full and written to **steady state**.

Fresh-out-of-box numbers hide garbage collection entirely. A new, empty drive has plenty of free blocks and no reason to copy valid pages yet.
takeaway: A benchmark on an empty drive measures a drive you'll never own.
deeper:
**Why mixed load:** GC is triggered by writes. A read-only test never forces the drive to reclaim blocks, so reads never collide with erases.

**Why 80% full:** A nearly full drive has fewer free blocks and must reclaim blocks that still hold many valid pages. That raises write amplification and GC time.

**Why steady state:** On its first pass, a drive writes into clean blocks. Only after the whole drive has been written and overwritten does GC run all the time. Steady state is the drive you will actually live with.

**Why p99.9:** At scale, requests fan out across many devices, so the rare slow device sets user-visible latency. An average can look excellent while the tail is terrible. And problems in the bottom storage layer, like tail latency, show up in every layer above.

quiz.q: A vendor shows p99.9 read latency from a brand-new drive running a 100% read workload. Name two reasons the number is too optimistic.
quiz.a: Read-only load never triggers garbage collection, and a new drive has free blocks so GC would barely copy anything anyway. Both hide the erase stalls a full, written drive hits.

mcq.q: Why does a read-only SSD benchmark understate real tail latency?
options: Without writes, garbage collection never collides with reads
Reads bypass the flash translation layer
Read-only tests always run at low queue depth
Reads wear flash faster than writes do
mcq.why: GC is triggered by writes. With none, no blocks are reclaimed and reads never wait behind an erase.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
hook: Hard drives grew from 4 TB to 30 TB. How many more random reads per second did they gain?

predict.q: Roughly how many random reads per second can one 7,200 RPM hard drive do?
options: About 80
About 800
About 8,000

title: ~80 random IOPS per HDD, flat for 20 years
body:
One random HDD read costs about one seek plus half a rotation. At 7,200 RPM the rotational wait averages 4.17 ms. Add a typical seek of about 8 ms and you get about 12 ms per I/O, or roughly 80 random **IOPS** (I/O operations per second) per drive.

That number barely changed in 20 years, because arms and spindles did not get faster. Capacity did.
takeaway: Disks are sold by capacity, but hot workloads are sized by IOPS.
deeper:
**The arithmetic:** One second divided by about 12 ms per operation is about 83, rounded to 80. Nothing in that formula depends on how many bytes the drive holds. The 8 ms seek is a typical figure, not from one datasheet.

**Density helps the wrong metric:** Each generation packs more data onto the platters, and enterprise drives now stream hundreds of MB/s, over 500 MB/s for some. But the head still moves and the platter still spins at the same speed, so random IOPS stay put.

**Sizing rule:** A workload that needs 800 random reads per second needs about 10 drives' worth of spindles, whether it fills 4 TB or 400 TB. That mismatch is the root of the IOPS-per-TB problem, and why the industry moved hot data to flash.

quiz.q: Your service needs 4,000 random reads per second from a 10 TB dataset. How many 7,200 RPM HDDs does the read rate require?
quiz.a: About 50. At roughly 80 random IOPS per drive, 4,000 / 80 = 50 drives, far more than the one drive 10 TB of capacity needs.

mcq.q: Why does a random HDD I/O take about 12 ms?
options: An ~8 ms seek plus a ~4.17 ms average rotational wait
A 12 ms interface round trip over SATA
The drive reads a whole 12 MB track each time
Firmware waits 12 ms to batch requests
mcq.why: Random I/O pays a typical 8 ms seek plus half a rotation at 7,200 RPM (4.17 ms): about 12 ms, or ~80 IOPS.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
hook: Every new generation of hard drive stores data more cheaply. What does each byte lose in the deal?
title: IOPS per TB: 20 at 4 TB, 2.7 at 30 TB

stat.label: random IOPS per TB on a 30 TB HAMR drive

body:
Every hard drive does about 80 random IOPS, whatever its size. So each terabyte's share shrinks as drives grow: 20 IOPS per TB at 4 TB, 6.7 at 12 TB, 3.3 at 24 TB and 2.7 at 30 TB.

Meta's Tectonic paper puts it directly: IOPS per hard drive stayed steady as density rose, so **IOPS per TB** declined over time.
takeaway: Each disk generation makes bytes cheaper to keep and harder to reach.
deeper:
**The economic tension:** Every generation lowers cost per GB. Backblaze saw $0.114 per GB in 2009 fall to $0.014 in November 2022. But it also lowers the access rate each stored byte can get. Data hot enough for 4 TB drives may be too hot for 24 TB drives.

**Three ways out:**
1. Move hot data to flash, which delivers vastly more IOPS per TB.
2. Reserve big HDDs for warm and cold data read with large sequential I/O, where throughput still scales.
3. Mix IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks, so one uses the spare IOPS and another the spare space. Meta's Tectonic does this.

**Without them:** Operators buy drives for IOPS and leave capacity empty. That is what happened to Meta's Haystack, whose effective replication factor rose from 3.6× to 5.3×.

quiz.q: A dataset gets 2,000 random reads per second per 100 TB and ran fine on 4 TB drives. Will it fit on 30 TB drives filled to capacity?
quiz.a: No. It needs 20 IOPS per TB, exactly what 4 TB drives give. 30 TB drives give only 2.7 IOPS per TB, leaving the workload about 7× short.

mcq.q: Why does IOPS per TB keep falling for hard drives?
options: IOPS per drive stays near 80 while capacity keeps growing
Denser platters make each seek take longer
SMR zones force every read to be sequential
Larger drives use slower interfaces
mcq.why: Random IOPS depend on seek and rotation, which haven't improved. Capacity grows, so each TB gets a smaller share.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
hook: Meta's photo store kept adding hard drives that stored no extra copies of anything. Why buy them?
title: Haystack bought disks for IOPS: 3.6× became 5.3×
body:
Meta's old hot-photo store, **Haystack**, became IOPS-bound. As drives grew, the photos on each drive demanded more random reads than its roughly 80 IOPS could deliver. So Meta bought extra drives just for their IOPS.

That pushed Haystack's **effective replication factor**, raw storage used per byte of data, from an ideal 3.6× to 5.3×, according to Meta's Tectonic paper.
takeaway: Buy disks for reads and you pay for empty space.
deeper:
**Why the factor rose:** Durability did not need more copies. The read rate needed more spindles. The extra drives' capacity largely went unused, so Meta paid for about 5.3 bytes of raw disk per byte of photos instead of 3.6.

**The mistake it illustrates:** Comparing media only on cost per GB. For hot data, cost per IOPS is often the real constraint, and a cheap-per-GB HDD that can't serve the read rate is not cheap.

**What came after:** Meta's later shared storage layer, Tectonic (described in 2021), mixes IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks, so cold data can fill space that hot workloads leave empty. Moving Meta's data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut its warehouse clusters by 10×.

**The wider pattern:** The same pressure is why the industry puts hot data on flash and keeps big HDDs for warm and cold data.

quiz.q: A hot store's ideal replication factor is 3.6×, but it runs at 5.3× and the disks are half empty. What's the likely diagnosis?
quiz.a: It is IOPS-bound. Extra drives were added for random-read capacity, not copies, so their space sits unused. Move hot data to flash or mix in capacity-hungry tenants.

mcq.q: What drove Haystack's effective replication factor from 3.6× to 5.3×?
options: Extra drives bought only for IOPS
A switch from erasure coding to 4 replicas
Correlated rack failures forcing more copies
Metadata growing faster than photo data
mcq.why: Haystack was IOPS-bound. Meta added drives for random-read capacity, adding raw disk that stored no extra copies.

section: How an HDD behaves, and the IOPS-per-TB problem
hook: Hard drives lose random-read power per TB every generation. How do big companies keep using them anyway?
title: 3 escapes from the HDD IOPS squeeze
body:
Because HDD IOPS per TB keeps falling, the industry uses three escapes. Put hot, randomly accessed data on flash. Keep big hard drives for warm and cold data read with large sequential I/O. And mix IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry **tenants** on the same disks so both resources get used, as Meta's Tectonic does.

Google's Colossus adds an SSD cache called **L4** and uses machine learning to place the hottest data on SSD while bulk data stays on HDD.
takeaway: Spend flash on heat and disk on bulk. Never pay flash prices for cold bytes.
deeper:
**Flash for heat:** NVMe SSDs serve random reads in tens of microseconds with deep parallel queues, so IOPS stop being the bottleneck. The price is higher cost per GB, worth paying only for the fraction of data that is actually hot.

**Sequential for disk:** Streaming reads avoid repeated seeks, so throughput scales with density even when IOPS do not. Dropbox writes 1 GB extents aligned to SMR zones, and Azure seals extents at about 1 GB. Both favor large sequential I/O.

**Mixing for balance:** Tenant mixing is a scheduling fix. One cluster storing hot blobs and cold warehouse data can spend the disks' IOPS on the first and their capacity on the second.

**In industry:** Google described the Colossus L4 cache in March 2025. Machine learning predicts which data is hot enough to deserve flash, so bulk data can stay on cheap disk.

quiz.q: One cluster serves a hot image index that uses all its disks' IOPS but 10% of their space. Another holds cold archives that fill space but barely read. What should you do?
quiz.a: Put both tenants on the same disks. The index spends the IOPS, the archives fill the idle capacity, and you stop buying drives that sit mostly empty.

mcq.q: What does Google's Colossus L4 do?
options: Caches hot data on SSD, placed by machine learning
Erasure codes cold data across four layers
Keeps metadata in four replicated regions
Moves cold data from HDD to tape
mcq.why: L4 is an SSD cache. Machine learning places the hottest data on SSD while bulk data stays on HDD.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
hook: One storage interface has no file names, no folders and no idea what your data is. Why do databases love it?
title: Block storage: numbered 4 KB slots, no names
body:
Storage is also defined by its interface: how a program asks for data. **Block storage** exposes a raw device, an array of fixed-size blocks, for example 4 KB, addressed by number, with no names. A file system or database on top decides what the blocks mean.

Examples: local NVMe, AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk and Ceph RBD. It is used mainly for databases and virtual machine disks.
takeaway: Block storage gives you control by giving you nothing else.
deeper:
**Its profile:** Block supports in-place updates of any block, has no namespace at all, just addresses, and typically offers the lowest latency of the three interfaces. Its scale limit is one volume.

**Why databases and VMs want it:** A database engine wants full control over layout, caching and write ordering, and block storage stays out of its way. A VM wants a virtual disk that looks like a real one, so the guest operating system can run its own file system on it.

**Over the network:** AWS EBS and Google Persistent Disk offer the same raw-device abstraction as a cloud service, and Ceph RBD does it on open-source storage.

**The limit:** A block device is just numbered slots, bounded by one volume. It does not become a shared namespace across many machines. That is what file and object storage add.

quiz.q: A team wants to run PostgreSQL directly on an object store to save money. Why does a database usually get block storage instead?
quiz.a: A database needs fast in-place updates of small pieces. Object storage replaces whole objects and typically takes tens of ms over HTTP; block updates any block in place at the lowest latency.

mcq.q: What namespace does block storage expose?
options: None: just numbered block addresses
A flat namespace of buckets and keys
A hierarchical directory tree
A per-volume table of file names
mcq.why: Block storage is a raw array of fixed-size blocks addressed by number. Names come from the file system or database on top.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
hook: Renaming a folder is instant on your laptop. Why do big distributed file systems often refuse to promise that?
title: POSIX files: familiar semantics, costly to distribute
body:
**File storage** exposes directories and files with open, read, write, rename and list. **POSIX** is the standard set of file semantics, such as atomic rename and byte-range writes. On one machine these are easy. Across thousands, every rename must look instantaneous to every client.

Full POSIX is expensive to distribute, so big distributed file systems often relax it. File storage serves HPC and AI training (Lustre, GPFS), shared home directories and Hadoop (HDFS).
takeaway: Every POSIX guarantee is a promise someone must coordinate at scale.
deeper:
**Its profile:** File storage sits between block and object. It updates byte ranges in place, uses a hierarchical namespace of directories, and typically has low to medium latency. Its scale limit is metadata server scaling.

**Why the tree is the bottleneck:** Every open, rename and directory listing needs a consistent view of the directory tree. An atomic rename of a directory must appear instantaneous to every client, which means coordinating whichever machines hold that metadata.

**Relaxing on purpose:** Many big systems trade guarantees for scale. GFS offered a record append with a relaxed consistency model that can even show duplicate records.

**Where it wins anyway:** Many readers sharing a familiar directory tree is exactly what HPC and AI training jobs want, so file storage still dominates there, along with legacy big-data workloads.

quiz.q: An AI training job needs thousands of workers to read one dataset through a normal directory tree. Which interface fits, and what limits its scale?
quiz.a: File storage, such as Lustre or GPFS. The limit is metadata: a shared hierarchical namespace must be coordinated, so metadata server scaling becomes the ceiling.

mcq.q: Why do large distributed file systems often relax full POSIX?
options: Guarantees like atomic rename need costly metadata coordination
POSIX forbids byte-range writes over networks
POSIX requires all data to live on one disk
Relaxed models give stronger durability
mcq.why: Atomic rename and consistent directory views must be coordinated across the machines holding metadata, which is expensive and limits scale.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
hook: Object storage can't edit a file in place or truly rename one. Why is it the default home for exabytes?
title: Object storage: flat keys, whole objects, huge scale
body:
**Object storage** exposes a flat namespace of buckets and keys. You PUT, GET (whole or a byte range) and DELETE whole objects. There is usually no in-place update and no real rename. Examples: Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob and Ceph RGW.

Those missing features are the point. A flat key space has no directory tree to coordinate, so it scales very high. It is the default for large, write-once data: photos, backups, logs and lakes.
takeaway: Give up editing and hierarchy, and you get almost unlimited scale.
deeper:
**Folders are an illusion:** Prefixes in keys look like folders, but they are just part of the key string. That is why "renaming a folder" is not a cheap operation: every key under it must change.

**The price:** Object stores are typically reached over HTTP with tens of milliseconds of latency, and changing one byte means replacing the whole object. That makes them a poor direct backing for a database.

**The perfect fit:** Immutable data. A photo is written once and read many times, never edited in place. In a billion-user app, photos and videos go to an object or blob store, replicated when new and erasure coded when warm. Logs and analytics data often land in an object store too.

**The split:** Object dominates large, immutable data; block dominates databases and VMs.

quiz.q: Photos sit in S3 under keys like users/42/album/…. A product change needs every album 'folder' renamed. Why is this expensive?
quiz.a: Prefixes aren't real folders; they are part of each key. With no real rename, every object under the prefix must be rewritten under a new key and the old one deleted.

mcq.q: How do you change one byte of an object in a typical object store?
options: Replace the whole object
Issue a byte-range write
Rename the object, then patch it
Append a delta to the key
mcq.why: Object storage usually has no in-place update. You PUT a new version of the whole object.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
hook: Pick the wrong storage interface and no amount of tuning saves you. What really separates the three?
title: Block vs file vs object: six trade-offs in one table
body: Each interface buys something by giving something up. Block: fixed-size blocks, in-place updates, no namespace, lowest latency, limited to one volume; used by databases and VMs. File: files in a directory tree, byte-range updates, low to medium latency, limited by **metadata server scaling**; used for HPC, AI training and Hadoop. Object: whole objects under flat keys, no in-place update, tens of ms over HTTP, very high scale; used for media, backups and lakes.
takeaway: Choosing an interface is choosing which semantics you refuse to pay for.
deeper:
**Read it as a spectrum:** Block is fastest and most flexible but bounded by one volume, and it has no names at all. File adds a shared hierarchical namespace, and that namespace is exactly what becomes the scaling bottleneck. Object gives up in-place updates and the lowest latency, uses named keys in a flat namespace, and scales very high.

**Match semantics to the job:**
1. A database needs in-place updates and low latency: block.
2. An AI training job needs many readers sharing a familiar directory tree: file, such as Lustre or GPFS.
3. A photo service needs billions of immutable blobs stored cheaply: object.

**The catch:** The lines are blurring. Object stores are gaining file-like features such as appends and hierarchical namespaces, so treat the table as a guide, not a law.

quiz.q: A colleague says object storage 'gives up hierarchy compared with block.' Correct them: what does object actually give up and gain relative to block?
quiz.a: Block has no namespace at all. Object gives up in-place updates and the lowest latency, and gains named keys in a flat, easily partitioned namespace that scales very high.

mcq.q: In the classic block/file/object comparison, which namespace does each interface have?
options: Block: none; file: hierarchical; object: flat
Block: flat; file: hierarchical; object: none
Block: none; file: flat; object: hierarchical
Block: hierarchical; file: flat; object: flat
mcq.why: Block has only numbered addresses. File has a real directory tree. Object keys are flat; prefixes only look like folders.

section: Block, file and object: the three interfaces
hook: Google shipped an object store with traits usually reserved for file systems. What made that possible?
title: Google Rapid Storage: an object store acting like files
body:
Object stores usually mean tens of milliseconds of latency, a flat namespace, and no way to add to an object without replacing it. Google's 2025 **Rapid Storage** for Cloud Storage breaks all three: sub-millisecond latency, unlimited appends and a hierarchical namespace.

It is built on **Colossus**'s stateful protocol. The line between file and object storage is blurring, because the interface is a layer on top of a shared storage system.
takeaway: Interfaces are categories, not laws. The layer underneath decides what's possible.
deeper:
**Against the usual table:** Typical object latency is medium, tens of ms over HTTP. The namespace is flat, with prefixes that only look like folders. Updates replace whole objects. Rapid Storage offers sub-millisecond latency, a hierarchical namespace, and unlimited appends.

**The enabler underneath:** Colossus underpins most Google Cloud products and is used by Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery. With one shared, durable storage layer already in place, Google can expose different interfaces on top of it. This is the layered-stack pattern big companies share.

**What it means for design:** Interface categories are guides. Workloads such as logs and AI training data that once needed a file system might be served by an object API with file-like features.

**The catch:** A new interface still sits on the same bottom layer, and problems down there show up in every layer above.

quiz.q: Your logging pipeline uses a distributed file system only for cheap appends and a directory tree. What 2025 change might let an object API serve it?
quiz.a: Google's Rapid Storage for Cloud Storage added unlimited appends, a hierarchical namespace and sub-millisecond latency to an object store, built on Colossus's stateful protocol.

mcq.q: Which feature set did Google's 2025 Rapid Storage bring to Cloud Storage?
options: Sub-millisecond latency, unlimited appends, hierarchical namespace
Tape-backed archive, eleven nines, flat namespace
In-place byte edits, POSIX locks, NFS access
Single-zone storage, 99.5% availability, lower price
mcq.why: Rapid Storage offers sub-millisecond latency, unlimited appends and a hierarchical namespace, built on Colossus's stateful protocol.

hook: S3 is designed so you essentially never lose an object. Does that mean you can always read it?
title: Eleven nines: S3's promise that your bytes survive
body:
**Durability** answers one question: will my data still exist? It is about not losing bytes, expressed as a probability of loss per year. Amazon S3 is designed for "99.999999999%", eleven nines.

It says nothing about whether you can reach the data right now. That is availability, a separate property. Durability comes from redundancy, automatic repair, and copies spread across failure domains so no single event destroys them all.
takeaway: Durable means not lost. It doesn't mean reachable.
deeper:
**Estimating it:** With 3 replicas, a 1.57% annual failure rate per disk, independent failures and one-day repair, the annual loss probability per object is about 1.7 × 10^-10. That is almost ten nines.

**Why the estimate lies:** Real failures are correlated. Google found failures often come in bursts tied to rack or multi-rack events. So placement across failure domains matters more than copy count.

**How S3 gets there:** S3 stores data across at least 3 availability zones by default for most storage classes. High durability rests on placement as well as redundancy.

**The catch:** Mixing up durability with availability or consistency leads to bad designs. Durable data can still be unreachable for a while; the only promise is that it hasn't been lost.

quiz.q: A zone outage makes some S3 One Zone-IA objects unreadable for an hour, then they return intact. Did S3 break its durability design?
quiz.a: No. Durability is about bytes not being lost, and none were. An hour of unreachability is an availability problem, a separate property with its own target.

mcq.q: What does a durability figure like eleven nines measure?
options: The chance stored data is not lost over a year
The share of requests that succeed
The chance a read returns the latest write
The fraction of time data can be reached
mcq.why: Durability is about not losing bytes, expressed as a probability per year. Reachability is availability; freshness is consistency.

hook: Two S3 storage classes share one eleven-nines durability design. One is reachable less often. How?
title: Same 11 nines of durability, 99.99% vs 99.5% uptime
body:
**Availability** asks: can I read or write my data right now? S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability. S3 One Zone-IA is designed for 99.5%. Both carry the same eleven-nines durability design.

So data can be extremely unlikely to be lost, yet noticeably more likely to be unreachable for a while. The two properties are tuned separately.
takeaway: Your users can't read durability. They read availability.
deeper:
**Why the gap:** One Zone-IA, as its name suggests, keeps data in a single availability zone, so a zone-level problem makes it unreachable even though the bytes are safe. S3 stores most classes across at least 3 zones by default, and a multi-zone copy can still answer when one zone has trouble.

**Most outages are short:** Much unavailability comes from transient events: a node rebooting, a top-of-rack switch failing, an upgrade taking nodes offline for seconds to minutes. In a one-year Google study of cells with 1,000 to 7,000 nodes, less than 10% of node unavailability events lasted longer than 15 minutes.

**Spread for both:** Google found that replicating across multiple cells greatly improves availability. Multi-zone and multi-region placement protect both properties at once. You can still have eleven nines of durability with only 99.5% availability.

quiz.q: A team picks S3 One Zone-IA for a user-facing image service because 'durability is identical to Standard.' What did they overlook?
quiz.a: Availability. One Zone-IA is designed for 99.5%, not 99.99%. The bytes are just as safe, but users will hit more periods when images can't be reached.

mcq.q: What availability is S3 Standard designed for, compared with S3 One Zone-IA?
mcq.why: Standard is designed for 99.99% availability and One Zone-IA for 99.5%, with the same eleven-nines durability design.

hook: Your write succeeded. A second later a reader sees the old value, or the same record twice. Is that a bug?
title: Consistency: will every later read see my write?
body:
Distributed storage keeps several copies, and copies can briefly disagree. **Consistency** asks: after a write succeeds, will every later read see it? **Strong consistency** means yes, always. Eventual consistency means readers may see old data for a while.

Relaxed models go further: GFS record append may even show duplicate records. None of these is a bug. Each is a guarantee a system chose, and your application must match it.
takeaway: A weaker guarantee isn't free. The application pays the difference.
deeper:
**The trade:** Strong consistency hides disagreement between copies from readers, usually at the cost of coordination. Weaker models are cheaper but push complexity onto applications, which must tolerate stale reads or deduplicate records.

**GFS as the example:** GFS's relaxed record append may show duplicates, so applications built on it must detect or tolerate duplicate records themselves.

**In a billion-user app:** Profiles need low latency and strong consistency for some fields, which points to a replicated database or key-value store with a cache. Messages need per-user ordering.

**Namespaces too:** POSIX's atomic rename is a strong consistency promise about the namespace, one reason full POSIX is expensive to distribute. Azure's 2011 storage paper is titled a highly available cloud storage service "with strong consistency", a claim that careful design can offer both.

quiz.q: A log pipeline built on GFS record append counts events and reports slightly too many. What's the likely cause, and the fix?
quiz.a: Record append's relaxed consistency can store duplicates. The application must deduplicate, for example by giving each record a unique ID and dropping repeats.

mcq.q: What does strong consistency guarantee?
options: Every read after a successful write sees that write
Data is never lost once written
Reads finish within a fixed latency
Duplicates are removed automatically
mcq.why: Strong consistency is about visibility: once a write succeeds, all later reads see it. Not losing data is durability.

hook: Data can be perfectly safe yet unreadable, or readable yet one power cut from gone. What does each look like?
title: Durable but unreachable, or reachable but fragile
body:
Durability and availability separate in both directions. **Durable but unavailable**: a rack's top-of-rack switch fails, or the rack is powered off. The disks are fine, so the bytes are safe, but nobody can reach them.

**Available but not durable**: a value accepted into one server's RAM cache but not yet written to disk. You can read it right now. A power loss would erase it forever.
takeaway: Ask what makes data unreachable, then ask what makes it gone.
deeper:
**Why not rebuild at once:** The durable-but-unavailable case is common, which makes instant rebuilding wasteful. The data is probably still there. Google found less than 10% of node unavailability events lasted longer than 15 minutes, so GFS waited 15 minutes before rebuilding a missing node's data.

**The write-path trap:** Acknowledging a write as soon as it reaches memory makes a system fast. But until the data is persisted and replicated, a single crash loses it. This is why DRAM holds caches and hot metadata, never the only copy.
