**Two separate questions:** In a design review, ask what is the smallest event that makes this data unreachable, and what is the smallest event that makes it gone. The answers often differ, and each needs its own fix.

quiz.q: A rack's switch dies, and its disks hold the only copies of some blocks. Is that a durability or an availability incident, and what would turn it into the other?
quiz.a: Availability: the bytes are intact but unreachable. It becomes a durability incident if those disks are destroyed or fail before the data is copied elsewhere.

mcq.q: Which is an example of data that is available but not durable?
options: A write held only in one server's RAM cache
Disks in a rack whose switch has failed
A One Zone-IA object during a zone outage
A tape cartridge sitting on a shelf
mcq.why: A RAM-only write can be read now, but a power loss erases it. The others are safe but unreachable.

hook: A storage node just vanished. Rebuilding its data right away sounds safest. Why did GFS deliberately wait?

predict.q: A storage node goes silent. Based on measured outage lengths, how long did GFS wait before rebuilding its data?
options: 15 minutes
No wait: it rebuilt immediately
24 hours

title: Wait 15 minutes before rebuilding: most outages heal
body:
When a node disappears, instant rebuilding sounds responsible. But in a one-year Google study of storage cells with 1,000 to 7,000 nodes each, less than 10% of **node unavailability events** lasted longer than 15 minutes.

So GFS waited 15 minutes before rebuilding data from a missing node. Rebuilding too early wastes network and disk I/O copying data for nodes that are about to come back.
takeaway: Most absences aren't deaths. Measure how long outages last before you react.
deeper:
**Two risks to balance:** Wait too little, and routine reboots, network blips and upgrades trigger heavy repair traffic for data that was never lost. That traffic competes with user I/O. Wait too long, and data sits with reduced redundancy, exposed to a second failure.

**Upgrades cause absences:** Azure notes that storage nodes go offline for seconds to minutes during upgrades. A system that rebuilt instantly would treat every rolling deploy as a disaster.

**The durability link:** The repair window is a key input to durability math. With a one-day window, the chance a given disk fails inside it is about 4.3 × 10^-5. The delay you pick affects both efficiency and durability.

**The method:** Google's study backs the delay with measured outage durations. Base yours on data too, not a guess.

quiz.q: Your cluster rebuilds a node's data the moment it stops heartbeating. During a rolling kernel upgrade, network traffic spikes and user latency climbs. Why, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: Each restart looks like a failure, so the system copies data for nodes that return minutes later. Add a rebuild delay based on measured outage lengths, as GFS did with 15 minutes.

mcq.q: Why did GFS wait 15 minutes before rebuilding a missing node's data?
options: Fewer than 10% of node outages lasted longer than 15 minutes
Allocating new disks took 15 minutes
Its lease timeout was 15 minutes long
Google's upgrades took exactly 15 minutes
mcq.why: Google measured that most node unavailability is short. Rebuilding sooner wastes network and disk on nodes that come back.

hook: The simplest way to protect data wastes two-thirds of your disks. Why is it still the default for hot data?
title: 3× replication: 200% overhead, 1-read repairs
body:
**Replication** keeps N full copies on different machines. With 3× replication, any two copies can be lost and the data survives. The overhead is 3×, or 200% extra space.

For that price, everything else is easy. Repair copies one surviving replica. Any replica can serve a read. A small write is just 3 I/Os, with no computation. That makes replication great for hot data, despite its cost.
takeaway: Replication overpays for disk to underpay for everything else.
deeper:
**The baseline:** Every other scheme is measured against 3× replication: 3 copies, 3.0× overhead, 2 losses tolerated, 1 fragment read to repair.

**Complete copies pay off:** Repair reads one copy, so it makes little network traffic and finishes fast, shrinking the time data sits with reduced redundancy. Any replica can serve a read, spreading hot-read load. A write just goes to three places.

**The weakness is scale:** Three copies means 3 exabytes of raw disk per exabyte of user data, versus 1.33 with an efficient erasure code. HDFS shows the gap: a 6-block file takes 18 blocks with 3× replication but only 9 with RS(6,3), which also tolerates 3 losses instead of 2.

**So both coexist:** Production systems use replication for new, hot or small data, and switch to erasure coding once data is sealed and cooler.

quiz.q: A message store takes huge numbers of tiny writes and repairs a node every day. Why is 3× replication a better fit here than RS(10,4)?
quiz.a: Each small write costs 3 I/Os instead of 14, and each repair reads one replica instead of 10 fragments. For hot, write-heavy data, those savings outweigh the extra disk.

mcq.q: With 3× replication, how many fragments must be read to repair one lost copy?
mcq.why: Every replica is a complete copy, so repair simply copies one survivor. Erasure codes must read k fragments.

hook: Cut data into 9 pieces, lose any 3, still rebuild it all, on half the disk of 3 copies. How?
title: Erasure coding: any k of k+m fragments rebuild it
body:
Full copies are expensive. **Erasure coding** (EC) splits data into k data fragments and computes m parity fragments. Any k of the k+m fragments can rebuild the data, so up to m can be lost. Overhead is (k + m) / k.

The common family is **Reed-Solomon**, written RS(k, m) here. RS(6,3) has 9 fragments, 1.5× overhead, and survives 3 losses. Some papers write the pair the other way around, so always check.
takeaway: Parity buys fault tolerance for a fraction of the disk. Repairs pay it back.
deeper:
**Four schemes compared:** RS(6,3) uses 9 fragments at 1.5×, tolerates 3 losses, and reads 6 to repair one. RS(10,4) uses 14 at 1.4×, tolerates 4, reads 10. RS(12,4) uses 16 at 1.33×, tolerates 4, reads 12. Azure's LRC(12,2,2) uses 16 at 1.33×, tolerates any 3 and many 4-failure patterns, and reads only 6.

**The HDFS example:** A file of 6 blocks takes 18 blocks with 3× replication, but only 9 with RS(6,3). Half the disk, and 3 losses tolerated instead of 2.

**The pattern to notice:** For classic Reed-Solomon, repair reads equal k. Wider codes save space but make every repair read more fragments over the network. That trade-off drives most erasure-code design, and it is why Azure built LRC to break it.

quiz.q: Compute the overhead, losses tolerated, and fragments read for one repair under RS(8,4).
quiz.a: Overhead (8+4)/8 = 1.5×. It tolerates any 4 lost fragments. A classic Reed-Solomon repair reads k = 8 fragments.

mcq.q: What are RS(10,4)'s overhead and loss tolerance?
options: 1.4×, any 4 lost fragments
1.4×, any 10 lost fragments
2.5×, any 4 lost fragments
1.25×, any 3 lost fragments
mcq.why: Overhead is (10+4)/10 = 1.4×. With m = 4 parity fragments, any 4 of the 14 can be lost.

hook: Erasure coding halves your disk bill and tolerates more failures. So why not use it for everything?

predict.q: One small write under RS(10,4) erasure coding. How many disk I/Os does it cost?

title: EC's three bills: repair traffic, small writes, slow reads
body:
Erasure coding saves space, but it sends three bills. **Repair traffic**: rebuilding one RS(6,3) fragment reads 6 fragments over the network; replication reads one copy. **Small writes**: RS(10,4) turns one small write into 14 I/Os instead of 3. **Degraded reads**: if a fragment is offline, the read must fetch k others and waits for the slowest of them.

All three get worse as codes get wider.
takeaway: Erasure coding is cheap to keep and expensive to touch.
deeper:
**Wider means slower repair:** Repair reads scale with k, so an RS(12,4) repair reads 12 fragments. That raises network traffic and the chance of hitting a slow or overloaded node. Slower repairs also stretch the time a stripe stays degraded and exposed.

**Small writes fit worst:** Replication writes three copies. EC must touch all k+m fragments of the stripe, which is why appending small records straight into an EC stripe is expensive.

**Degraded reads hit the tail:** A normal read fetches the fragment it needs. A degraded read waits for k fragments, and the slowest one sets its latency, the same fan-out problem as SSD tails.

**The flip side:** Reconstruction can also rescue latency. Azure starts a parallel reconstruction when a fragment read looks slow and returns whichever finishes first.

quiz.q: You erasure code a hot key-value store with RS(10,4) to save disk. Users complain writes are slow and reads spike during node failures. Explain both.
quiz.a: Each small write updates 14 fragments instead of 3 copies. With a fragment offline, reads must fetch 10 others and wait for the slowest, so tails spike.

mcq.q: How many I/Os does one small write cost under RS(10,4), versus 3× replication?
options: 14 vs 3
10 vs 3
4 vs 1
14 vs 1
mcq.why: A small write must update every fragment in the RS(10,4) stripe, 10 data plus 4 parity, versus three copies.

hook: Replication is fast to write; erasure coding is cheap to store. Do production systems have to pick one?
title: Write replicated, seal, then erasure code later
body:
Production systems take both. **Azure**'s stream layer writes 3 replicas, seals an extent when it reaches about 1 GB, erasure codes it lazily in the background, then deletes the replicas. **Tectonic**'s blob storage does the same: replicated quorum appends for small writes, re-encoded to RS(10,4) once a block is sealed.

Fast writes while data is hot, cheap storage once it is done changing.
takeaway: Replicate while data changes. Encode once it stops.
deeper:
**Why replicate first:** Small appends cost 3 I/Os replicated but 14 with RS(10,4). Fresh data is also usually the hottest, so replication's fast reads help too.

**Why sealing is the turn:** A sealed extent or block is immutable, so there are no more small updates to pay for. One large encode is efficient, each fragment can be written sequentially to its target disk, and the replicas can be deleted to reclaim space.

**Why lazy:** Encoding is deferred work. It can be scheduled when resources are free instead of sitting on the write path, which keeps user-facing latency low.

**The same shape elsewhere:** Photos and videos in a billion-user app follow it too: replicated when new, erasure coded when warm. For the same data, age picks the scheme.

quiz.q: A new system erasure codes every write immediately with RS(10,4). What two costs could a replicate-then-seal design avoid?
quiz.a: Small writes costing 14 I/Os instead of 3, and encoding work on the write path. Replicating keeps appends cheap; encoding sealed, immutable data in the background is one efficient pass.

mcq.q: When does Azure's stream layer erasure code an extent?
options: After it is sealed at about 1 GB, lazily in the background
On every write, before acknowledging it
Only after a replica fails
As soon as the extent is created
mcq.why: Azure writes 3 replicas, seals the extent at about 1 GB, then encodes it in the background and deletes the replicas.

hook: Microsoft found a standard code that hit its exact overhead target. Why wasn't it good enough?

predict.q: Standard RS(12,4) gives 1.33× overhead. How many fragments must it read to repair one lost fragment?

title: Why Azure rejected RS(12,4): 12 reads per repair
body:
Microsoft wanted 1.33× storage overhead for Azure. Standard Reed-Solomon RS(12,4) delivers exactly that: 12 data fragments plus 4 parity, 16 in total.

The problem was repair. Rebuilding one lost fragment means reading 12 others, and every extra read raises the chance of hitting a slow or hot node. Repairs get slower and more expensive. Microsoft's answer was a new code: **Local Reconstruction Codes** (LRC).
takeaway: The overhead number is half the spec. Repair cost is the other half.
deeper:
**The wide-code trade:** Large k lowers overhead, but a Reed-Solomon repair reads k fragments. As k grows, every repair gets more network-heavy and involves more machines, and the slowest of them decides when it finishes.

**Repairs are constant:** At a 1.57% annual failure rate, a large fleet loses drives every day. Servers also go offline for seconds to minutes during upgrades. Each event triggers reconstruction reads, for permanent repair and for degraded reads served while a fragment is missing.

**The target:** RS(6,3) repairs with 6 reads but costs 1.5×. RS(12,4) reaches 1.33× but needs 12 reads. Microsoft wanted the overhead of the second with the repair cost of the first.

**Why it mattered:** Microsoft said erasure coding could cut storage cost by over 50% and its datacenter footprint by half.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes RS(20,4) to push overhead down to 1.2×. What happens to single-fragment repairs, and why might that hurt hot data?
quiz.a: Each repair reads 20 fragments instead of 6 to 12. More reads mean more network traffic, a higher chance of a slow node, and longer degraded windows.

mcq.q: What was Azure's problem with RS(12,4)?
options: Each single repair read 12 fragments
Its overhead was too high at 1.5×
It tolerated only 2 lost fragments
It needed 20 fault domains per rack
mcq.why: RS(12,4) hit 1.33× overhead, but repairing one fragment read 12 others, raising traffic and the chance of a slow node.

hook: Azure wanted 1.33× overhead with half the repair reads of the standard code. What's the trick?
title: LRC(12,2,2): two local groups of 6, two global parities
body:
**LRC(12,2,2)** splits 12 data fragments into two local groups of 6. Each group gets one local parity. Then 2 global parities cover all 12. That is 16 fragments, so overhead is 16/12 = 1.33×.

The payoff is repair. A lost data fragment is rebuilt from its own group: the other 5 data fragments plus the group's local parity. Just 6 reads, not 12.
takeaway: Fix the common failure locally. Save the global machinery for rare ones.
deeper:
**Two jobs, two parities:** Local parities make the common case, a single lost fragment, cheap: it is fixed within a group of 6. Global parities protect against larger failures across the whole stripe.

**The table row:** LRC(12,2,2) has 16 fragments and 1.33× overhead, tolerates any 3 failures and many 4-failure patterns, and reads 6 fragments to repair one. RS(12,4) tolerates any 4 but reads 12 for every repair.

**Placement still counts:** Azure lays out LRC fragments across 20 fault domains and 10 upgrade domains. No single rack failure or rolling upgrade takes out too many fragments of one stripe.

**The catch:** LRC does not survive every 4-failure pattern, while RS(12,4) does. The trade is cheap everyday repairs in exchange for that guarantee.

quiz.q: In LRC(12,2,2), data fragment 3 of group A is lost. Which fragments are read to rebuild it, and how many?
quiz.a: The other 5 data fragments in group A plus group A's local parity: 6 reads. Group B and the global parities are not needed.

mcq.q: How many fragments does LRC(12,2,2) read to repair one lost data fragment?
mcq.why: A lost data fragment is rebuilt from its local group: the other 5 data fragments plus that group's local parity.

hook: 0.17 sounds like a rounding error. On an exabyte of data, what does shaving it off overhead actually buy?
title: 0.17× less overhead = 170 PB of disk you never buy
body:
Compared with RS(6,3), Azure's LRC(12,2,2) keeps the repair cost the same, 6 fragment reads, but cuts overhead from 1.5× to 1.33×. Microsoft says it is also more durable than 3 replicas.

As a ratio, 0.17× looks tiny. On one exabyte of user data, it is 170 petabytes of disk you do not buy, plus the servers, power and space to run them.
takeaway: At scale, the second decimal place is a procurement budget.
deeper:
**Why engineers chase fractions:** Per exabyte stored, 3× replication needs 3 exabytes of raw disk and 1.33× needs 1.33. That is a 1.67-exabyte gap. Even the small step from 1.5× to 1.33× is 170 petabytes.

**Having it both ways:** Wide codes normally save space by making repairs slower and more network-heavy. LRC reaches the overhead of a wide code while keeping repair reads at 6, the same as the narrower RS(6,3).

**More durable, too:** LRC tolerates any 3 failures and many 4-failure patterns, versus 2 for three replicas. Spread across 20 fault domains, it gave Azure cheaper and more durable storage at once.

**The catch:** Those savings apply to data that sits still long enough to be encoded. Hot, changing data still pays replication's price first.

quiz.q: Your org stores 5 EB on RS(6,3). Moving to an LRC at 1.33× keeps repair reads at 6. How much raw disk does the switch free?
quiz.a: 0.17× of 5 EB, about 850 PB, with no increase in repair reads.

mcq.q: Versus RS(6,3), what does LRC(12,2,2) change?
options: Overhead drops from 1.5× to 1.33×; repair stays at 6 reads
Repair drops from 6 reads to 3; overhead stays 1.5×
Overhead drops to 1.2×; repair rises to 12 reads
Loss tolerance rises to 6; overhead stays 1.5×
mcq.why: LRC keeps the 6-read repair of RS(6,3) while cutting overhead by 0.17×, which is 170 PB per exabyte.

hook: Two teams pick different erasure codes for the same cluster, and both are right. How?
title: Pick the erasure code for the failure you fear most
body:
The right code depends on the failure you fear most. **Wide codes**, with large k, save space but make repairs slower and more network-heavy. That stretches the time a stripe stays **degraded**: missing a fragment and exposed to further losses.

For hot data, the number of repair reads and degraded-read tail latency often matter more than the last few percent of overhead. For cold archives, overhead may be the bigger fear.
takeaway: Optimize for the failure you fear, not the metric that's easiest to quote.
deeper:
**Name the fear:** If cost is the fear, as with cold archive data, a wider code with lower overhead makes sense. If slow reads during failures are the fear, as with hot data serving users, a narrower code or plain replication keeps repairs and degraded reads fast.

**The mechanics:** Classic Reed-Solomon repair reads k fragments. RS(12,4) reads 12, RS(6,3) reads 6. More reads mean more network traffic, a higher chance of a slow or busy node, and a longer repair. All that time, the stripe has less margin before data loss.

**The user's view:** A degraded read must reconstruct from k fragments and waits for the slowest of them.

**What real systems do:** They keep hot data replicated and encode once data is sealed and cooler. Azure invented LRC rather than simply adopting the widest code available.

quiz.q: One team stores 10-year compliance archives; another serves hot thumbnails. Both ask for an erasure-code recommendation. What do you tell each?
quiz.a: Archives: a wide code, since cost dominates and slow repairs hurt no user. Thumbnails: replication or a narrow code, since repair reads and degraded-read tails decide user latency.

mcq.q: Why can a wide erasure code be risky for hot data?
options: Repairs read more fragments, stretching degraded time and read tails
Wide codes tolerate fewer lost fragments
Wide codes need more raw disk per byte
Wide codes cannot be spread across racks
mcq.why: Large k means each repair and degraded read touches more fragments, so it is slower and more exposed to slow nodes.

hook: Three replicas on ordinary disks. How safe does back-of-envelope math say your data is?

predict.q: 3 replicas, 1.57% annual disk failure rate, independent failures, 1-day repair. Roughly how many nines of durability does the math give?
options: Almost ten nines
About five nines
About three nines

title: Back-of-envelope: 3 replicas look like ten nines
body:
Assume 3 replicas on 3 different disks, a 1.57% annual failure rate per disk (Backblaze 2024), independent failures, and 1 day to rebuild a lost replica. A first failure among the 3 disks happens with probability about 0.047 per year.

Data is lost only if the second disk fails in the first repair window and the third in the second. That gives an annual loss probability per object of about 1.7 × 10^-10. Almost ten nines.
takeaway: A durability number is only as honest as its independence assumption.
deeper:
**The chain:**
1. Chance a given disk fails in a 1-day window: 0.0157 / 365 ≈ 4.3 × 10^-5.
2. Chance of a first failure among 3 disks per year: 3 × 0.0157 ≈ 0.047.
3. Second disk fails in the first window, third in the second: ≈ 2 × 4.3 × 10^-5 × 4.3 × 10^-5 ≈ 3.7 × 10^-9.
4. Annual loss per object: 0.047 × 3.7 × 10^-9 ≈ 1.7 × 10^-10.

**The levers it reveals:** Faster repair shrinks both windows, and each window's tiny probability is multiplied in, so repair speed pays off twice. Lower failure rates help too. Another replica multiplies in another tiny factor.

**The catch:** This is an optimistic estimate, not a guarantee. It assumes disks fail independently, and in practice they do not.

quiz.q: In the three-replica estimate, repair time drops from 1 day to half a day. Roughly what happens to the annual loss probability, and why?
quiz.a: It falls about 4×. Loss needs two more failures, each inside a repair window. Each window's probability halves, so their product drops to about a quarter.

mcq.q: In the estimate, why is the chance a disk fails in a 1-day window about 4.3 × 10^-5?
mcq.why: Spread the 1.57% annual failure rate evenly over 365 days: 0.0157 / 365 ≈ 4.3 × 10^-5 per day.

hook: The durability math says almost ten nines. One ordinary event can wipe out all three copies. What is it?
title: Why the ten-nines math lies: failures come in bursts
body:
The simple estimate multiplies small probabilities, which only works if disks fail independently. They don't. Google found that a large fraction of failures happen in bursts, mostly tied to rack or multi-rack events, and concluded that accounting for **correlated failures** is the critical element of availability models.

A single rack power event destroys all three replicas at once if they share the rack. Placement, not just copy count, decides real durability.
takeaway: Copies that share a fate count as one.
deeper:
**Why the math breaks:** The model multiplies three tiny, independent probabilities. If one event can take out every copy, the loss probability is roughly the probability of that single event, which is far larger than the product.

**Google's finding:** Google's 2010 study found that most large failure bursts are rack or multi-rack events, and that modeling correlated failures is the critical element.

**Where correlation hides:**
1. Shared racks and top-of-rack switches.
2. Shared power feeds.
3. A firmware bug that hits every drive of one model.
4. Upgrades that take many nodes offline together.

**The fix:** Design placement around failure domains. Spread copies or fragments across racks, power domains, zones and regions, so the smallest event that destroys every copy is very rare.

quiz.q: Your durability model shows ten nines, but all three replicas of each object sit in one rack. What is your real loss risk roughly equal to?
quiz.a: The chance of a single rack event, such as a power failure, that destroys the rack. That is far higher than three independent disk failures in a short window.

mcq.q: Why is the independent-failure durability model optimistic?
options: Real failures come in correlated bursts, like rack events
It ignores the cost of repair traffic
Its 1.57% failure rate is far too high
It counts parity fragments as data
mcq.why: One rack, power or firmware event can take out several copies together, so multiplying independent probabilities badly understates risk.

hook: Your data has copies on three different disks. How many kinds of failure could still take all three?
title: Failure domains: disk, host, rack, power, zone, region
body: Three copies on three disks can still die together if those disks share something. A **failure domain** is a set of components that can fail together for that reason. They nest: disk (media errors, head crash, firmware), host (motherboard, NIC, kernel, storage daemon), rack (top-of-rack switch, rack power), power domain (shared feed or PDU), zone (power, cooling, network) and region (natural disaster, regional control-plane bug).
takeaway: Your real exposure is the smallest domain that holds every copy.
deeper:
**Each level, a bigger blast radius:** Copies on different disks survive a disk failure. If those disks share a host, a motherboard failure takes them all. If the hosts share a rack, a top-of-rack switch failure hides them all. And so on up to regions.

**The habit to build:** For any piece of data, find the smallest failure domain that contains all its copies. That domain's failure rate, not the disks', is your real exposure. Put as a question: what is the smallest event that destroys all copies?

**Not all domains are physical:** Software creates correlated failures too. A firmware bug can hit every drive of one model. A control-plane bug can hit a whole region. Upgrades form their own domain, which is why Azure tracks upgrade domains alongside fault domains when placing erasure-coded fragments.

quiz.q: Three replicas sit on three disks in three different hosts, all in one rack on one power feed. What is the smallest failure domain holding all three?
quiz.a: The rack. A top-of-rack switch or rack power failure takes out every copy, even though the disks and hosts are separate.

mcq.q: What makes a set of components one failure domain?
options: They share something, so one event can fail them together
They have the same capacity and speed
They hold replicas of the same object
They sit behind the same load balancer
mcq.why: A failure domain is defined by a shared dependency: a host, switch, power feed, site or firmware whose failure hits all of them.

hook: One server's motherboard dies. How many disks' worth of data just became unreachable?

predict.q: A single dense storage server fails. How many of its disks go offline with it?
options: Exactly 1
2 to 4

title: One host dies, 30 to 100 disks go with it
body:
**Correlated failures** take out many components at once. A host failure takes out all 30 to 100 of its disks together. A top-of-rack switch failure hides a whole rack, even if every disk inside is fine. A firmware bug can hit every drive of one model at the same time, anywhere in the fleet.

So counting copies is not enough. You must know what those copies share.
takeaway: Before counting copies, list what they share.
deeper:
**Hosts, big and immediate:** A dense storage server holds dozens of disks, so copies on different disks of the same host offer no protection against it. It also creates a large repair job, since every chunk on those disks may need rebuilding.

**Switches, usually availability:** A top-of-rack switch failure leaves data intact but unreachable. It is the classic durable-but-unavailable case. If all replicas share that rack, the data is out of reach until the switch is fixed.

**Firmware, the sneakiest:** It crosses physical boundaries. Copies spread across racks and zones can still share a drive model. The same logic applies to bugs in storage daemons or kernels.

**The conclusion:** This is why Google called correlated failures the critical element in availability models.

quiz.q: You spread replicas across three zones, but every drive is the same model on the same firmware. Which failure can still hit all copies?
quiz.a: A firmware bug in that drive model. It can strike every such drive at the same time, wherever it sits, so spreading across zones doesn't protect against it.

mcq.q: Why is a top-of-rack switch failure usually an availability event rather than a durability event?
options: The disks are intact but nobody can reach them
The switch erases data as it fails
Switches hold the only copy of metadata
Switch failures last under a second
mcq.why: The rack's disks keep their bytes. Only the path to them is gone, so data is durable but unavailable until the switch is fixed.

hook: An RS(6,3) stripe survives 3 lost fragments. Spread it over 3 racks and one rack dies. How safe is it now?
title: RS(6,3) on 3 racks vs 9: spread across failure domains
body:
The first rule against correlated failures: spread copies or fragments so no single event takes more than the code can tolerate. HDFS wants **RS(6,3)** across at least 3 racks, ideally 9 or more. On 3 racks, each holds 3 fragments, so losing one rack uses the code's entire tolerance. On 9 racks, a rack failure costs one fragment.

Azure lays out LRC fragments across 20 fault domains. Tectonic survives host, rack and power-domain failures.
takeaway: No domain should hold more pieces than the code can lose.
deeper:
**The rule stated exactly:** For 3× replication, the three copies must sit in three separate domains at every level you care about. For erasure coding, no domain may hold more than m fragments of a stripe.

**Azure's version:** Azure builds each rack as a separate fault domain with redundant networking and power. It lays out LRC fragments across 20 fault domains and 10 upgrade domains, so rolling upgrades never take down too many fragments of one stripe.

**Tectonic's version:** Meta's Tectonic is built to survive host, rack and power-domain failures.

**The catch:** Wide codes make placement harder. A 16-fragment stripe needs many independent domains to keep each one under its limit, which is why Azure spreads LRC across 20. The wider the stripe, the more domains you need.

quiz.q: You place an RS(10,4) stripe across 7 racks, 2 fragments per rack. How many rack failures can it survive, and why?
quiz.a: Two. Each rack failure costs 2 fragments, and RS(10,4) tolerates 4 lost fragments. A third rack failure would mean 6 lost.

mcq.q: Why does HDFS prefer RS(6,3) across 9 or more racks rather than 3?
options: On 9 racks a rack failure costs 1 fragment, not 3
Nine racks make each repair read fewer fragments
RS(6,3) needs 9 racks to compute parity
Three racks cannot physically hold 9 fragments
mcq.why: On 3 racks, one rack failure uses all 3 losses the code tolerates. On 9, it costs one, leaving margin.

hook: Nothing broke. No disk failed. Your own deploy still took data offline. How?
title: Rule 2: your rolling upgrade is a failure domain
body:
To a storage system, a node restarting for an upgrade looks exactly like a failed one. Azure notes that storage nodes go offline for seconds to minutes during upgrades. A **rolling deploy** that restarts too many nodes at once takes several copies or fragments of the same data offline together.

That is a correlated failure you caused yourself. Azure tracks **upgrade domains** alongside fault domains for exactly this reason.
takeaway: Your deploy tool is part of your durability design.
deeper:
**Why planned feels safe:** Nothing is broken, so maintenance feels harmless. But if enough nodes holding the same stripe restart together, reads for that data become degraded or unavailable. A real hardware failure during the deploy could push it into data loss.

**Azure's answer:** Define upgrade domains and place LRC fragments across 10 of them. Upgrading one domain at a time never takes out more fragments than the code can tolerate.

**The rebuild-delay link:** Google's one-year study found less than 10% of node unavailability events lasted over 15 minutes, so GFS waited 15 minutes before rebuilding a missing node. Upgrade restarts are exactly this kind of short absence. Rebuilding on every restart would flood the network with pointless repair traffic.

**The lesson:** Pace deploys against how data is placed.

quiz.q: A deploy script restarts 20% of storage nodes at a time, chosen at random. Why can this cause unavailability even with erasure coding?
quiz.a: A random batch can include several nodes holding fragments of the same stripe. If more fragments are offline than the code tolerates, that data is unreadable until nodes return.

mcq.q: Why does Azure place LRC fragments across 10 upgrade domains?
options: So upgrading one domain never takes too many fragments offline
So each upgrade finishes in under 15 minutes
So upgrades can skip nodes holding parity
So 10 nodes can upgrade in parallel
mcq.why: Restarting nodes are offline for seconds to minutes. Spreading fragments across upgrade domains keeps each rollout step within the code's tolerance.

hook: Racks and power feeds are covered. What protects your data from losing a whole datacenter, or a region?
title: Rule 3: zones and regions cover the biggest disasters
body:
The largest failure domains, datacenters, availability zones and regions, need the widest spread. Amazon S3 stores data across at least 3 availability zones by default for most storage classes. Google found that replicating across multiple storage **cells** greatly improves availability.

That protects against a whole datacenter losing power, cooling or network, and against natural disasters or regional control-plane bugs.
takeaway: The bigger the disaster you plan for, the farther your copies must travel.
deeper:
**The price is distance:** Zones in one region are close enough for fairly fast replication. Regions can be continents apart, and light takes real time to cross an ocean. Multi-region placement adds latency to any synchronous write and costs cross-region bandwidth.

**S3 shows the payoff:** S3 keeps most classes in at least 3 zones. S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability. One Zone-IA, a single-zone class as its name suggests, is designed for 99.5%. Both share the eleven-nines durability design.

**Google's version:** Replicating across multiple cells means a problem in one cell does not take the other copies with it.

**The catch:** Wide spread protects durability and availability, but every write that must wait for a far copy pays for it in latency.

quiz.q: A payments ledger must survive a regional disaster, and product wants every write confirmed in a second region. What will that cost?
quiz.a: Latency and bandwidth. Each synchronous write waits for data to reach a distant region, bounded by the speed of light, and cross-region traffic costs money.

mcq.q: Across how many availability zones does S3 store data by default for most storage classes?
options: At least 3
Exactly 1
At least 2
At least 5
mcq.why: S3 spreads most classes across at least 3 AZs, so no single zone holds every copy.

hook: Your design doc says 'three replicas.' Against one very common event, how many copies do you really have?

predict.q: Three replicas sit in one rack. Against a rack power failure, how many copies' worth of protection do you have?
options: About one
About two
Three

title: Three replicas in one rack is really one replica
body:
The common mistake is counting replicas without checking placement. "Three replicas" in one rack are roughly one replica against a rack failure. A single top-of-rack switch or rack power event takes all three offline or destroys them together.

The copy count looks safe on paper while the real protection is minimal. Always ask: what is the **smallest event** that destroys all copies of this data?
takeaway: Count failure domains, not copies.
deeper:
**The math, broken in practice:** The independent-failure estimate assumed 3 replicas on 3 disks failing independently and produced almost ten nines. Put those disks in one rack, and one rack event, far more likely than three independent disk failures in a short window, loses everything.

**Ask at every level:**
1. Copies share a host: the smallest event is a motherboard failure.
2. They share a power feed: a PDU fault.
3. They share a drive model: a firmware bug.
4. They share a region: a regional disaster or control-plane bug.

**Erasure coding too:** A 9-fragment RS(6,3) stripe across only 3 racks puts 3 fragments in each rack. One rack failure spends the code's entire tolerance.

**The rule:** Correlated failures dominate real durability, so placement matters more than replica count.

quiz.q: A reviewer sees 'RF=3' in a design and approves it. What single question should they have asked, and why?
quiz.a: What is the smallest event that destroys all copies? If all three share a rack or power feed, one event loses everything, so RF=3 alone means little.

mcq.q: Which review question best exposes a replica-placement mistake?
options: What is the smallest event that destroys all copies?
How many replicas does each object have?
What is the drive's annualized failure rate?
How long does a single repair take?
mcq.why: Copy count hides shared racks, power and firmware. Asking for the smallest event that kills every copy reveals the real exposure.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
hook: Big companies store exabytes, yet none runs one storage system to do it. What do they build instead?
title: Big tech builds a storage stack, not a storage system
body: Big companies don't build one storage system. They build a stack, where each layer solves one problem and exposes a simpler interface upward. From the bottom: hardware; storage node software (chunk or extent servers); a **distributed storage layer** (Colossus, Tectonic, HDFS, Azure stream layer); databases, object stores and data lake tables; and applications.
takeaway: Solve each hard problem once, in one layer, then build on it.
deeper:
**The middle branches:** On top of the storage layer sit databases and key-value stores (Spanner, Bigtable, ZippyDB, Cassandra, MySQL) and object and blob stores (S3, GCS, Azure Blob, Ambry). Data lake table formats (Iceberg, Hudi, Delta) are built on files, higher in the stack. Applications such as feed, messaging, search, ads and ML training pick whichever service fits.

**One app, one foundation:** Profiles go to a database, photos to a blob store, analytics to lake tables. All of them rely on the same distributed storage layer for durability.

**The benefit:** Replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing live in the storage layer, so a database team never reimplements them.

**The catch:** Coupling. When the bottom layer has problems such as tail latency, every layer above feels them.

quiz.q: A database team plans to build its own replication and disk-repair logic on raw servers. In a layered stack, what should they do instead?
quiz.a: Store their files on the shared storage layer, which already handles replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing, and spend their effort on transactions and indexes.

mcq.q: Which layer handles replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing?
options: The distributed storage layer, such as Colossus
The application layer, such as feed or ads
The hardware layer, such as HDDs and NICs
The lake table layer, such as Iceberg
mcq.why: The storage layer turns thousands of nodes into one durable pool and handles redundancy and repair for everything above it.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
hook: At the bottom of a big storage stack, servers don't know what a file or a user is. What do they store?
title: The bottom layers: priced per TB, storing anonymous chunks
body: The bottom two layers are hardware and storage node software. **Hardware** (HDDs, SSDs, NICs, racks, power) is chosen on three numbers: cost per TB, IOPS per TB and power per TB. **Storage node software** runs on each server and stores chunks (GFS, Tectonic) or extents (Azure), as files on a local file system or directly on the raw device. Tectonic nodes store chunks as files on XFS.
takeaway: The lower the layer, the less it should know.
deeper:
**Cost per TB:** Favors large HDDs, whose price fell from $0.114 per GB in 2009 to $0.014 in November 2022.

**IOPS per TB:** Favors flash, because HDD random IOPS stay near 80 per drive while capacity grows.

**Power per TB:** A big fleet pays to power every drive it runs. Tape uses no power on a shelf, a point in its favour for archives.

**Deliberately simple nodes:** Node software knows about chunks or extents, blocks of data identified by ID, not files, users or tables. Higher layers decide what chunks mean and where copies go. Storing chunks as files on XFS, as Tectonic does, reuses a mature file system. Writing to the raw device skips a layer and gives full control, useful for things like aligning writes to host-managed SMR zones.

quiz.q: You're choosing drives for a cold-archive cluster and a hot-index cluster. Which hardware metric dominates each?
quiz.a: Cold archive: cost per TB, plus power per TB, so big HDDs. Hot index: IOPS per TB, so flash, since HDD random IOPS stay near 80 per drive.

mcq.q: How do Tectonic storage nodes store chunks?
options: As files on XFS
Directly on raw SMR zones
As objects in S3
As rows in MySQL
mcq.why: Tectonic nodes store chunks as files on the XFS local file system, reusing a mature file system instead of managing raw devices.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
hook: Thousands of servers, disks dying daily. How does the database on top see one reliable pool?
title: The storage layer: thousands of nodes, one durable pool
body:
The **distributed storage layer** turns thousands of storage nodes into one durable pool with a namespace. It handles replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing, so nothing above has to.

Google's Colossus underpins most Google Cloud products and is used by Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery. Meta has Tectonic. Azure has the stream layer inside each storage stamp. HDFS plays this role in Hadoop deployments.
takeaway: Durability should be one team's hard problem, not every team's.
deeper:
**Where the durability machinery lives:** This layer places replicas or fragments across failure domains, notices when nodes disappear, waits before rebuilding (GFS used 15 minutes), and moves data to balance load and capacity.

**Where encode-later runs:** Azure's stream layer writes 3 replicas, seals an extent at about 1 GB, then erasure codes it lazily with LRC. Tectonic uses replicated quorum appends for small writes and re-encodes to RS(10,4) once a block is sealed.

**The hard part:** The namespace. Metadata scaling is the central problem of distributed file systems, from GFS and HDFS to Colossus and Tectonic.

**Shared layer, shared effects:** Everything above inherits this layer's behavior, good and bad. Colossus, for example, adds an SSD cache called L4 and uses machine learning to place the hottest data on SSD.

quiz.q: A new team at Google needs durable storage for its service. Why wouldn't they build erasure coding and repair themselves?
quiz.a: Colossus already turns thousands of nodes into one durable pool and handles replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing. Services like Spanner and Bigtable build on it instead.

mcq.q: Which job belongs to the distributed storage layer?
options: Repairing data after node failures
Running SQL transactions
Choosing a store for each data type
Serving the feed to users
mcq.why: The storage layer handles replication, erasure coding, repair and rebalancing. Transactions belong to databases; store choice belongs to applications.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
hook: A database on a shared storage layer never replicates its own disks. So what is it actually for?
title: Databases and object stores add meaning, not durability
body:
Above the shared storage layer, services add **semantics**: transactions, indexes, key lookups, object APIs. They don't reimplement durability; they store their data in the layer below. Azure's partition layer, which serves Blobs, Tables and Queues, stores everything in the stream layer.

At the top, applications pick the right service for each data type: a database for profiles, a blob store for photos.
takeaway: Let the bottom keep bytes safe and the top decide what they mean.
deeper:
**The menu:** Databases and key-value stores such as Spanner, Bigtable, ZippyDB, Cassandra and MySQL. Object and blob stores such as S3, GCS, Azure Blob and Ambry. Data lake table formats such as Iceberg, Hudi and Delta, which sit on files.

**Google makes it concrete:** Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery all use Colossus. Their teams can focus on query processing, transactions and indexing while Colossus keeps the bytes safe.

**Apps choose per data type:** Profiles go to a replicated database with a cache. Messages go to an LSM-based database. Photos go to a blob store. Logs flow through a log system such as Kafka into a DFS or object store. Analytics lands in lake tables.

**The catch:** Semantics on top cannot hide problems below. Tail latency in the storage layer surfaces in every service.

quiz.q: Azure Tables and Azure Blobs look like very different products. What do they share underneath?
quiz.a: Both are served by Azure's partition layer, which stores everything in the same stream layer. Durability comes from that shared layer, not from each product.

mcq.q: Where does Azure's partition layer store its data?
options: In the stream layer
On local disks of each partition server
In a separate Blob cluster
In HDFS
mcq.why: The partition layer serves Blobs, Tables and Queues and stores everything in the stream layer below it.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
hook: Building every service on one shared storage layer saves huge effort. What does each one inherit in return?
title: Layering's deal: free durability, shared tail latency
body:
Durability is hard and should be solved once. A database team writes files to the shared storage layer and gets durability for free, without building replication, erasure coding or repair.

The price is **shared fate**. Problems in the bottom layer show up everywhere above. If the storage layer suffers tail latency spikes, every database, object store and application built on it inherits those spikes.
takeaway: Shared infrastructure means shared fate. Fix the bottom and everyone gets faster.
deeper:
**What sharing buys:** Every team uses the same efficient erasure coding and placement logic. The disk pool is shared, so capacity and IOPS can be balanced across tenants.

**What sharing costs:** The bottom layer's weaknesses propagate. SSD garbage-collection spikes, HDD IOPS limits, degraded reads during repair and slow nodes during upgrades all become latency the higher layers must absorb. A request at the top may fan out into many reads at the bottom, so a small tail problem below can become a large one above.

**Why tail fixes matter:** Hedged reads and Azure's parallel reconstruction of slow fragments help every service at once.

**The stakes:** An upgrade or bug in the shared layer can hit every service together, which makes it one of the largest failure domains you own.

quiz.q: Several unrelated services report p99 spikes at the same moment. They share nothing but the storage layer. Where do you look first, and why?
quiz.a: The shared storage layer. Its problems, such as GC stalls, repairs or a rolling upgrade, reach every service above, and fan-out turns a small tail below into a big one above.

mcq.q: What is the main downside of building every service on one shared storage layer?
options: Its problems, like tail latency, reach every service above
Each service must reimplement replication
Services can no longer share disk capacity
Durability drops below eleven nines
mcq.why: Layering solves durability once, but the bottom layer's weaknesses propagate to every service built on it.

section: The layered storage stack at a big company
hook: Google, Microsoft and Meta built their storage separately. What design did all three end up with?
title: Three giants, one design: a shared storage layer
body:
Google (Colossus), Microsoft (the Azure stream layer, described in 2011) and Meta (Tectonic, described in 2021) **converged** on one architecture: a single shared storage layer with specialized services on top.

The payoff can be large. When Meta moved its data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic, it cut its number of warehouse clusters by 10×.
takeaway: When rivals converge on one design, the pressure behind it is real.
deeper:
**Same pressures, same answer:** Failure is routine, durability is hard, and cost at exabyte scale rewards pooling. Three companies facing those pressures landed in the same place.

**Why pooling pays:** A shared layer like Tectonic can mix IOPS-hungry and capacity-hungry tenants on the same disks, using both resources instead of leaving one idle. For Meta's warehouse, data that once lived in many HDFS clusters now shares far fewer, larger pools of disks. Tectonic's blob storage also re-encodes sealed blocks to RS(10,4), 1.4× overhead instead of 3×.

**How far it reaches:** Colossus underpins most Google Cloud products, including Spanner, Bigtable and BigQuery. It also enables newer products like Rapid Storage, with sub-millisecond latency and a hierarchical namespace built on Colossus's stateful protocol. One layer, many products on top.

quiz.q: A company runs a separate HDFS cluster for each analytics team, each with idle IOPS or idle space. What does Meta's experience suggest?
quiz.a: Consolidate onto one shared storage layer. Meta moved its warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic and cut warehouse clusters by 10×, pooling capacity and IOPS across tenants.

mcq.q: What happened when Meta moved its data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic?
options: Its warehouse cluster count fell by 10×
Its replication factor rose to 5.3×
Its storage overhead fell to 1.33×
Its query latency fell by 10×
mcq.why: Consolidating onto the shared Tectonic layer cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10×.

section: Mapping the running example to storage types
hook: Profiles and messages are both tiny records. Why does a billion-user app store them in different databases?
title: Profiles vs messages: same size, opposite access patterns
body:
Profiles and messages are both small records, but they flip the read/write ratio. **Profiles** number in the billions and are read-heavy. They need low latency and strong consistency for some fields: a replicated database or key-value store, on SSD with a DRAM cache.

**Messages** are write-heavy. They need high write throughput and per-user ordering: a log-structured (LSM) database on SSD. Both are hot and mutable, so both live on flash with replication.
takeaway: Size tells you little. The read/write ratio picks the database.
deeper:
**Profiles, read-first:** Reads far outnumber writes, so a DRAM cache absorbs most of them while the database behind it provides durability and consistency. Some fields, such as settings, may need strong consistency so a user sees their own change right away.

**Messages, write-first:** An LSM database turns many small writes into large sequential ones. That suits flash, where large sequential writes give the lowest write amplification and the least wear. Per-user ordering matters because a conversation must display in sequence.

**Why not HDD:** Random access would quickly exhaust an HDD's roughly 80 IOPS, the same IOPS-per-TB squeeze that made Meta's Haystack IOPS-bound.

**The shared rule:** Small, hot, mutable data lives on flash with replication. The read/write ratio then decides which database sits on top.

quiz.q: A chat app keeps messages in the same read-optimized, cache-fronted store as profiles. Writes start lagging. Why, and what fits better?
quiz.a: Messages are small and write-heavy, so a read-optimized design struggles. An LSM database turns many small writes into sequential ones, giving the write throughput messages need, on SSD.

mcq.q: Which store fits message data in a billion-user app?
options: An LSM database on SSD
An object store on HDD
A DRAM-only cache
A tape archive with SSD cache
mcq.why: Messages are small and write-heavy. An LSM database turns small writes into sequential ones and runs on flash.

section: Mapping the running example to storage types
hook: Photos, logs, analytics and backups look nothing alike. What do they have in common?
title: Photos, logs, analytics, backups: big bytes, cheap media
body: The large data types go to cheaper media. **Photos and videos** are write-once blobs, hot then cold: an object or blob store, replicated when new and erasure coded when warm, on HDD with SSD cache and a CDN. **Logs and events** are append-only and huge: a log system like Kafka landing in a DFS or object store. Analytics and ML data lives in a data lake. Backups go to an archive tier or tape.
takeaway: Big, immutable and sequential is the signature of cheap disk and erasure coding.
deeper:
**Media streams:** Photos and videos need cheap durability, high throughput and a CDN, so HDD bulk with an SSD cache. Logs and events need append throughput and cheap retention: SSD for the hot part, HDD for bulk.

**Scans:** Analytics and ML data needs aggregate throughput, low cost and table formats. It lives in a data lake on an object store or DFS, on HDD bulk with SSD or NVMe caches for training.

**Archives:** Backups and compliance archives are rarely read but kept for years. They need the lowest cost and immutability: an archive object tier or tape, with an HDD cold tier or tape as media.

**The common thread:** Large size, mostly immutable data and sequential access suit HDD and erasure coding. Profiles and messages complete the picture: small, hot, and on replicated SSD.

quiz.q: A new feature stores 50 PB of user videos that are hot for a week, then rarely watched. Sketch the storage lifecycle.
quiz.a: Object or blob store: replicated while new and hot, erasure coded once warm, on HDD with an SSD cache and a CDN serving popular videos.

mcq.q: Where do backups and compliance archives typically go?
options: An archive object tier or tape
A replicated database on SSD
An LSM database on NVMe
A DRAM cache with HDD spill
mcq.why: They are rarely read but must be kept for years, so they need the lowest cost and immutability: an archive tier or tape.

section: Mapping the running example to storage types
hook: Strip away the product names and a big company's storage splits into two worlds. What are they?
title: Hot on replicated flash, cold on erasure-coded disk
body:
One pattern runs through a big app's storage. Small, hot, mutable data lives on **flash with replication**: profiles and messages. Large, cold, immutable data lives on **HDD with erasure coding**: aged photos and videos, logs, analytics files and backups.

Everything in between, caches, databases, object stores, lakes and tiering, exists to move data between those two worlds as it is written, read, cools down and ages.
takeaway: Most storage engineering is moving bytes from hot to cold at the right time.
deeper:
**Why hot means flash and replicas:** Hot data needs IOPS and low latency, and HDD IOPS per TB keeps falling. Hot data is also written and read often, where replication's 3-I/O small writes, fast repairs and any-replica reads beat erasure coding's 14 I/Os per small write under RS(10,4).

**Why cold means disk and EC:** Cold data needs cheap capacity, and HDDs at $0.014 per GB (Backblaze, November 2022) with large sequential I/O deliver it. Cold data is immutable and rarely read, so EC's small-write and degraded-read costs rarely bite, and 1.33× to 1.5× overhead instead of 3× saves huge amounts of disk.

**Where the effort goes:** The transitions. Sealing extents and encoding them in the background, caching hot items in DRAM or SSD, and tiering data down to archive or tape as it ages.

quiz.q: A file is written, read heavily for a month, then barely touched for years. How should its storage change over its life?
quiz.a: Start replicated, on flash or behind a flash cache, while hot. Once sealed and cooling, erasure code it on HDD. As it ages further, tier it to archive or tape.

mcq.q: Why does cold, immutable data suit erasure coding better than hot data?
options: EC's costs hit small writes and degraded reads, which cold data rarely triggers
EC reads are faster than replica reads
Cold data needs strong consistency, which EC provides
EC works only on HDD, where cold data lives
mcq.why: Erasure coding is expensive for small writes and degraded reads. Immutable cold data rarely triggers those, so its low overhead wins.

section: Map of the rest of the book
hook: Metadata, caches, tape, compliance: over a dozen hard topics lie ahead. How do they fit together?
title: The road ahead: 13 topics climbing one storage stack
body:
The topics ahead climb the same stack. First the storage layer: **distributed file systems**, where scaling metadata is the theme, then object storage. Then the services on top: block, local and Kubernetes storage; databases and storage engines; caching tiers; lakes, tiering and archival.

Then what cuts across everything: scaling, operations and migrations, reliability and DR, compliance and security, cost, company case studies, and the senior staff lens.
takeaway: Learn storage bottom-up: bytes first, services next, judgment last.
deeper:
**The storage layer:** Distributed file systems cover GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic, Azure, Ceph and Lustre. Object storage explains how S3, GCS and Azure Blob are built.

**The services:** Block storage covers network block devices, local NVMe, CSI and persistent volumes. Storage engines compare B-trees and LSM-trees, RocksDB and sharded databases. Caching covers DRAM and flash caches, hot keys, and caches as a reliability risk. Lakes cover hot, warm and cold tiers, lifecycle and tape.

**The cross-cutting concerns:** Scaling covers sharding, rebalancing, hot spots and capacity planning. Operations covers safe rollouts and moving exabytes. Reliability covers durability math, scrubbing, backups and multi-region. Compliance covers encryption, keys, deletion and residency. Cost covers cost per useful byte, media mix and utilization.

**The synthesis:** How each big company assembled its stack and why, then leading design reviews and making long-term bets.

quiz.q: Your biggest pain is a file system whose namespace server keeps hitting memory limits. Which topic on the road ahead addresses it, and what is its central theme?
quiz.a: Distributed file systems. Their central problem is scaling metadata, worked through GFS, Colossus, HDFS, Tectonic, Azure, Ceph and Lustre.

mcq.q: Which topic has scaling metadata as its central theme?
options: Distributed file systems
Object storage
Caching tiers
Cost and efficiency
mcq.why: Metadata scaling is the central problem of distributed file systems such as GFS, HDFS, Colossus and Tectonic.

hook: Strip storage infrastructure down to three forces. Which three shape every design decision?
title: Failure, physics and cost shape every storage design
body: At big-tech scale, failure is routine: 300,000 drives at 1.57% AFR lose about 13 a day, so repair must be automatic. Media latency spans about six orders of magnitude, from DRAM (~100 ns) to HDD (~10 ms) to tape. SSDs cannot overwrite in place, which explains their wear and tail spikes. HDD IOPS per TB keeps falling, pushing hot data to flash.
takeaway: Assume disks die, respect physics, and price every useful byte.
deeper:
**Interfaces and properties:** Block, file and object have different semantics. Object dominates large immutable data, block dominates databases and VMs, file dominates HPC, AI training and legacy big data. Durability, availability and consistency are different properties: you can have eleven nines of durability with only 99.5% availability.

**Redundancy:** Erasure coding cuts overhead from 3× to 1.33× to 1.5×, but costs more repair traffic, more I/Os for small writes and worse degraded-read latency. So systems write replicated and encode after sealing. Azure's LRC(12,2,2) keeps 1.33× but rebuilds a lost fragment from 6 reads instead of 12.

**Placement and structure:** Correlated failures (rack, power, upgrades, firmware) dominate real durability, so placement matters more than replica count. Big companies build one shared storage layer (Colossus, Tectonic, Azure stream layer) with databases, object stores and lakes on top.

**The test:** Four questions catch most bad designs: access pattern, durability target, latency including the tail, and cost per useful byte.

quiz.q: A proposal keeps hot user sessions on 3× replicated HDDs, all in one rack, and quotes median latency. Name three problems.
quiz.a: HDD IOPS per TB is too low for hot data; one rack means one rack event loses every copy; and the median hides the tail. Use flash, spread placement, and set p99 targets.

mcq.q: Why do systems write replicated first and erasure code after sealing?
options: Small writes are cheap replicated; sealed data encodes efficiently
Erasure coding needs three replicas as its input
Replicas are more durable than any erasure code
Data must be sealed before anyone can read it
mcq.why: Replication makes small appends cheap (3 I/Os vs 14 for RS(10,4)). Once sealed and immutable, one efficient encode runs and replicas are deleted.
